Up to 50% of people admit cheating on their partner.

People who are low on conscientiousness are more likely to cheat on their partner, research finds.

People who are not conscientious are careless, badly organised and find it hard to resist temptation.

People who are more extraverted are also more likely to cheat on their partner, the researchers found.

It is probably because extraverted people have a wider social circle and so more opportunities to cheat.

Also, extraverts are impulsive, sensation-seekers who can easily succumb to their desires.

“Extroverts may be inclined to cheat to obtain stimulation and prevent boredom.

#9742. Flowise Chatflow API Keys Do Not Boundary the Stored Credentials

A Flowise chatflow can be protected by an API key and still execute nodes that use stored third-party credentials. The key controls who can call the flow, not what secrets the flow can reach. A review that stops at the public endpoint misses the credential store, the node permissions, and the external systems the flow can access.

Flowise documentation describes chatflow-level authorization with a generated API key and an Authorization header. It also states that an unauthenticated public chatflow API or embedded chat can be accessed by anyone. The environment documentation says Flowise encrypts third-party API keys as credentials using an encryption key, and SECRETKEY_PATH controls where the secret key is stored.

The first zone is the person or application calling the chatflow. The second is the running flow, including tools, HTTP nodes, vector stores, and model providers. The third is the credential store and its encryption key. An API key in the first zone should not imply access to the third.

Inventory each flow's exposed endpoint, authentication setting, allowed users, and external integrations. Identify which credential IDs it references without printing the secret values. Limit the flow's ability to call arbitrary HTTP endpoints or shell tools unless that capability is reviewed.

Store SECRETKEY_PATH on persistent protected storage with restricted filesystem permissions. Back it up separately from the database and test restoration. If an attacker obtains both the encrypted credential database and the encryption key, the UI length difference for a credential API key does not provide protection.

Rotate the encryption strategy through a planned migration, not by replacing the key in place without a re-encryption process. Confirm that worker and web processes use the same key and that a restart does not create a new key without the operator noticing.

An embedded chat or public API may be a legitimate front door. Add authentication at the reverse proxy or application layer when the flow can spend money, query private data, or call internal systems. Apply rate limits, request-size limits, timeout controls, and output filters. Log the flow ID and caller identity without logging complete prompts that may contain personal data.

Test whether a chatflow API key can be used against another flow. Test an unauthenticated request to each public and private path. Check CORS, cache headers, and whether the browser exposes the key in client-side code.

The count-only measurement used sub_type=all, page 1, and page size 1. app="Flowise" returned 40,899, title="Flowise" returned 42,439, and http.body="Flowise" returned 485,939. The body count is large and can include documentation, examples, and unrelated references. A public Flowise fingerprint is a discovery lead, not proof that a credential is exposed or that a flow is exploitable.

Correlate owned instances with cloud tags, DNS, certificate names, and expected business units. If a development instance is public by mistake, disable its external access before investigating individual flows.

Create a flow inventory with owner, purpose, external credentials, data sources, and endpoint authorization. Review it when a new tool node is added, not only at deployment. The security boundary is the combination of caller identity, flow capability, and secret access.

#9740. Exactly-Once Publishing on Cloudflare D1 Without Transactions

I run a small daily game, Costcodle, where everyone guesses the price of the same Costco item each day. Just after midnight UTC, a scheduled job publishes the answer page of every puzzle that has finished. It is a tiny job, and for a while it was the part of the system I trusted least.

The reason was a migration. I was merging two Cloudflare Workers, one for the website and one for scheduled jobs, into a single Worker. Until the old one was deleted, both would fire the same cron string at the same moment, against the same database. I wanted three guarantees to survive that overlap:

The database is Cloudflare D1, and that is where it gets interesting.

D1 gives you batch(). The documentation is clear about what it does: "Batched statements are SQL transactions," and if a statement in the sequence fails, D1 "aborts or rolls back the entire sequence" (D1 Database API).

That is a strong guarantee about errors. It says nothing about statements that succeed and do nothing. An UPDATE whose WHERE clause matches zero rows is not an error, so the batch carries on and commits whatever the other statements did.

What the Worker binding does not give you is an interactive transaction: open it, read a row, decide in your own code, then write, all under one lock. So the natural pattern, "check that I still hold the lease, then write," has a gap in it. Between the read that checks and the batch that writes, another job can take over. If the batch then runs three statements and only some of their conditions still hold, you get exactly the state you were trying to avoid: an item marked published with no page, or a page with no revision bump.

The fix I ended up with has two parts. A lease with a fencing token decides who may publish. A guard repeated inside every statement of the final batch makes sure a writer that lost the lease changes nothing at all.

Leases live in a job_leases table: a key such as publication:1121, an owner id, an expiry and a fence counter. Taking a lease is a single upsert (simplified from the real repository):

If nobody holds the key, the insert creates it with fence 1. If the current lease has expired, the conflict branch hands it to the new owner and increments the fence. If the lease is still live, the setWhere clause matches nothing, no row comes back, and the caller skips that item for now. Each run gets a fresh random owner id, so two Workers firing the same cron look like two independent owners competing for the same keys. My leases last 180 seconds.

A lease alone is not enough, and the reason is well known. Martin Kleppmann's How to do distributed locking puts it plainly: "you need to include a fencing token with every write request to the storage service." A holder can stall long enough for its lease to expire, someone else takes over, and then the first holder wakes up and writes anyway. HackerNoon has two good deep dives on this failure, The Fencing Gap: Why Your Distributed Lock Isn't Safe and Building Distributed Leases With Consensus, Heartbeats, and Fencing Tokens. Both arrive at the same rule: the storage layer has to check the token itself.

In my case the storage layer is the same SQLite database that holds the lease, which makes that check unusually cheap. It can be part of the write.

Every write that depends on the lease carries this condition:

If another job has taken over, the fence no longer matches, and the condition is false inside the very statement that would have written.

The final publish batch takes this further. Its first statement inserts or updates the page with INSERT ... SELECT ... WHERE , and the guard re-checks everything the job verified earlier, in SQL: the lease, the ledger item's state, the question bank version, that the image is ready, and that the page is still at the content version the job expected (plain optimistic concurrency). That statement also writes a random commit_token. Every statement after it is conditioned on that token having landed:

If the guard is false, statement 1 writes nothing, so the token never lands, so statements 2 and 3 match zero rows as well. The zero propagates through the whole batch. The job reads the page back, sees a different token, and reports lease_lost or conflict without having changed anything.

The same guard enforces two one-way rules I care about. A page that search engines may index never goes back to noindex, and a page that has its product photo never loses it. Both are expressed as conditions on the existing row, so a stale or confused writer cannot undo them.

There is a test for the exact gap described earlier. It lets the job finish its read batch, then has a second repository take over the lease before the final batch runs. The call returns lease_lost, and the test then checks the database: no page row, a publication revision still at 0, and the ledger item still marked as processing.

Statement 3 above is the second half of the design. Every change to published content, a new page, an updated page or a withdrawal, bumps one global publicationRevision in the same atomic batch that made the change. A rerun that changes nothing public leaves it alone.

The edge cache uses that number as part of every key for content that depends on publications:

Each request reads the current revision from the primary database first and only then looks in the cache. After a publication, every request builds a key that has never been stored, misses, renders the fresh page and stores it under the new key. The old entries are still there. Nothing will ever ask for them again, and they age out on their own.

This matters more on Workers than it might elsewhere. The Cache API documentation notes that "the contents of the cache do not replicate outside of the originating data center," and that cache.delete "only purges content of the cache in the data center that the Worker was invoked." A purge from inside a Worker is a local operation. Changing the key is global by construction.

The general pattern of versioned cache keys is covered well in The Many Layers of Caching. What surprised me was the one case it did not cover.

In my game, yesterday's puzzle stays playable for a 10 minute grace window after midnight UTC, and its answer must not become public until that window ends. At 00:10 UTC, yesterday's answer becomes publishable. No publication has happened at that instant, so the revision has not changed.

If a "not published yet" response had been cached at 00:09 with a 300 second lifetime, it would keep answering until 00:14 under a perfectly valid key. So content entries get a lifetime of the smaller of 300 seconds and the time left until 00:10 UTC. If your data has any moment where visibility changes without a write, a revision-keyed cache needs the same treatment: find that moment and make sure no entry lives across it.

The price of the whole scheme is one database read per cacheable request, to learn the revision. For a site of this size that is a good trade.

The pattern of putting every condition inside the write also works without a lease. After each game, the client can report the result for the day's shared stats. The rules are: one row per game session, at most 50,000 rows per puzzle, and a dense slot number for each row. All three are handled by one statement:

SQLite runs a single statement atomically and D1 serializes writes to a database, so two concurrent reports cannot take the same slot, a duplicate session inserts nothing, and a full puzzle inserts nothing. There is no window between the check and the write because there is no separate check.

One detail took a test to get right. The bare max(slot) sits alone in its own scalar subquery. SQLite's MIN/MAX optimization can answer a single MAX() over the leading column of an index "by doing a single index lookup rather than by scanning the entire table," and wrapping it in a larger expression loses that. A test seeds 49,999 rows for one puzzle and asserts that the next insert reads fewer than 20 rows. For the ON CONFLICT clauses used throughout, the SQLite UPSERT documentation is the reference.

Unit tests cover each piece: concurrent lease claims, two concurrent compare-and-set commits where only one wins, and the takeover between preflight and commit. The test I trust most runs on the real stack. An integration run starts the actual Worker with D1 and R2 and fires the publish cron twice at the same instant, the way the old and new Workers would during the merge. Then it fires the hourly compensation job twice at once, several rounds in a row.

The result: one daily quota row, six pages each published exactly once at content version 1, a publication revision of exactly 6, and seven source images each downloaded and stored exactly once. Two more simultaneous compensation runs afterwards find nothing to do and change nothing.

You can see the pages this pipeline publishes in the Costcodle answers list.

How do you get exactly-once behavior out of a store that only offers batches? I would like to hear what other people have built on D1 or plain SQLite.

Costcodle is an independent fan game. It is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by Costco Wholesale Corporation.

#9739. Monthly Instagram Reports for SMM Clients

It was the last working day of the month, the day I send my clients their Instagram reports. I had a coffee, a half-finished report and a script that had worked fine the previous month. Then it died on a login challenge, and I spent the next hour re-authenticating an account instead of sending anything. I'm a freelance social media manager who writes just enough Python to get into trouble, and that hour was when I started asking whether I should be maintaining this at all.

Once a month I pull stats for each client's account (followers, recent posts, how the posts did) and turn them into a report. The volume is small, but the deadline is real and the numbers have to be right, because clients read them.

I used instagrapi first, and I'd still recommend it in the right situation. It's free, it's well maintained, and it gives you a lot of control. For a hobby project or a one-off script it's hard to beat.

None of that is the library's fault. It's how that approach works.

I moved the collection step to HikerAPI, a hosted REST API. You send your key in an x-access-key header and call an endpoint. It's pay-per-request, starting at about $0.001 per request, and there are 100 free requests to try it. I used those to compare the output with what I see in the app before changing anything.

That's the whole login flow: there isn't one. My report script went from managing sessions and retries to looping over a list of usernames and saving each response to a file, so a failed run only re-fetches what's missing.

For my use, small and deadline-driven, the hosted API removed the part that kept breaking. If you're a developer who enjoys controlling every layer, or you run a lot of accounts yourself, instagrapi may still be the better fit.

Disclosure: the provider offers free credits for write-ups like this one, so weigh my opinion accordingly. The comparison above comes from what I actually ran into.

What's your setup for recurring Instagram reports? Still running your own, or have you handed it off?

#9738. Transformers Model Integration Contracts

On July 30, 2026, Transformers enabled PyTorch's scaled dot-product attention (SDPA) for T5. As a side effect, UMT5's decoder could attend to future tokens. During training, it could peek at the answer it was supposed to predict. Nothing crashed, and the bug stayed in main for almost two months.

When we later replayed those commits, a small UMT5 model running on CPU flagged it on every one of them. This post is about that model and the tests built around it.

Transformers supports over 750 model types, and its test suite is big: 88,000+ CPU tests on main, plus 200,000+ GPU tests in a daily run. Model tests are only part of it: we also test pipelines, training, distributed execution, quantization and attention kernels.

The integration tests load real checkpoints and exercise the model's API on real hardware. Running all of that on every PR would mean keeping a lot of GPUs busy all day long, which isn't practical. By the time a scheduled run finds a regression, it may already be in main.

Our approach is to shrink the model instead. We build a fixture: a small model made from the real checkpoint's configuration, with fewer and narrower layers but every kind of layer it has, and its tokenizer and processor files unchanged. It is published once, then reused. We run "fast integration tests" against it on a cheap CPU runner. In our CPU study, the experimental UMT5 fixture used 66 MB of weights; the source checkpoint is 1,227 MB.

This also covers very large models: some don't fit on our standard GPU runners, but their fixtures run on CPU.

Model integrators already build tiny test models (Transformers' tiny-random-* checkpoints). We wanted a common recipe, and checks that go beyond loading the model and running a forward pass. The UMT5 bug would have passed a forward pass just fine.

Fixtures won't replace full integration tests, but on PRs they give us a chance to catch bugs before they reach main.

transformers-mic is a proposed standard for packaging these tests. A Model Integration Contract (MIC) has three parts:

The contract holds if running the usage path on the fixture still produces the baselines.

A contract covers an architecture and a usage path, not a single checkpoint: compatible checkpoints can share a fixture, while each keeps its own expected results. We publish them in huggingface-mic.

For example, the SmolLM contract generates from prompts such as "The capital of France is" and compares its token IDs with a recorded answer. After loading the model and tokenizer, the generation code is, simplified to one prompt:

It also compares training loss, checks that gradients are finite and verifies that an optimizer step changes the weights. See the full usage.md.

A fleet dataset on the Hub pins each MIC to a frozen revision, along with the package versions used to record its baselines. Each CI run records the fleet revision it used, so we can reproduce it later.

On a PR, we pick MICs based on the files the patch changes.

We replayed frozen MICs over five months of Transformers commits. The small UMT5 fixture flagged the regression from its introduction on July 30, 2026 until its fix on September 28. Label log-probabilities differed from the reviewed baseline by 1.22 and training loss by about 0.20.

One detail mattered: the contract used SDPA, the default attention path. Running only the eager attention variant missed the bug. A fixture only helps if it goes through the same code as the real checkpoint.

We then reverted the fix on a proof branch in Transformers' CI. The check failed with the same differences, and the selected T5 contract's runner step took 13.4 seconds on CPU, excluding setup.

The replay results and the CI demo have the measurements and reproduction details.

The first recipe was simple: make the dimensions smaller and keep fewer layers. That wasn't enough for mixed architectures. Keeping two layers is no use if both use sliding attention and the full-attention layers disappear.

We also keep the original weights file format. Otherwise we would skip the conversion code that runs when a user loads the real checkpoint. The full recipe has more detail.

The Llama 4 Scout shrink report shows what this looks like on a big model. 108.6 billion parameters become 44.7 million. The vision stack goes from 34 layers to 2 and the language stack from 48 to 4, keeping the checked layer kinds and MoE routing style.

Our CLI, tmic, creates the contract and builds the fixture. For a new model, an LLM drafts the usage code and manifest, and CPU and GPU runs measure the candidate baselines. The LLM drafts; it doesn't approve. Changed expectations require human review.

To try it on your machine, use your source checkpoint in place of org/model:

It drafts the contract, builds the fixture and records its baselines on your machine, asking you to review each step, and stops before uploading anything. For a new model, the draft comes from an LLM through Inference Providers, billed to your own account (--bill-to ''). The CLI docs cover the individual steps.

We used agents to build MICs across model families. When they hit an edge case, we fixed the recipe itself rather than the one fixture, with help from model experts. The published models and remaining gaps are in the coverage space.

With random weights, our Whisper fixture barely responded to changes in the audio. It ran, but that made it a poor test of the audio path.

So we trained it on a few tones paired with words such as "red" and "green". We weren't teaching it speech recognition, just making audio changes visible in its outputs. In our weight-initialization study, the random Whisper fixtures caught 18 of 24 injected faults. The overfit fixtures caught all 24.

That gives us two ways to build the weights:

The Whisper result doesn't settle which is better. Those were synthetic faults, and we haven't found a real regression caught only by the overfit version. Both versions missed an assisted-decoding bug that the real Whisper checkpoint exposed.

So we keep random weights when they pass the checks, and overfit when we need better sensitivity or readable answers. Training takes seconds, but it is one more step that can fail to converge, and one more thing to maintain. The comparison has the results for both.

As of November 1, 2026, the MIC job in Transformers CI reports failures without blocking PRs. Whether it should block depends on things we haven't measured yet:

We also don't know how many bugs, like the Whisper assisted-decoding one, only show up with real weights, or whether overfitting catches real bugs that random weights miss.

Coverage is still partial, across model families and the APIs people use. When a regression slips through, we can add the missing usage path and replay it on the broken and fixed versions. We'll keep existing tests until their coverage is accounted for.

Finally, we'd like to link original Hub model pages to their MICs, so a developer or an agent using a checkpoint could start from an example tested on that checkpoint, its environment and its expected outputs.

Want to help? Pick an uncovered model from the coverage space, try the tmic workflow, and contribute a usage path or review a generated contract.

#9735. Order Beats Randomness: Bisecting Test Pollution in Agent Patches

Most tests labeled "flaky" in an agent-patch pipeline are not nondeterministic at all. They are order-dependent: they pass alone, and fail after some other test leaves shared state behind. Randomization masks that. Bisection names it.

The distinction matters because the two failures have opposite remedies. A genuinely random failure earns a temporary freeze. An order-dependent failure earns a fixture fix — and freezing it instead quietly locks in a bug that resurfaces the next time an agent inserts a file.

What follows is a reproduction-first workflow: prove the target passes alone, delta-debug the smallest prefix that breaks it, then classify the result before anyone touches a quarantine list.

Agents insert files. Runners collect files in a fixed order, usually alphabetical by path. An agent that adds tests/test_auth_refresh.py next to an existing tests/test_z_session.py changes execution order for everything in between, without editing a single existing test.

Session-scoped fixtures are the usual carrier: a cache, a temp database, an env var, a module-level client. The new first test warms it in a way the old second test does not expect.

Then the pipeline sees test_rotate fail at head, pass at base, and pass when re-run alone. The label "flaky" follows. That label is close to meaningless — the test never was nondeterministic, the schedule changed.

Before bisecting, prove the target passes in isolation, repeatedly, at head.

Three outcomes, and only one of them belongs in this workflow:

-p no:randomly disables the plugin if your suite uses one. Without it, the isolation run and the pollution run are not comparable, and the whole exercise produces noise.

Now find the smallest set of tests that, run before the target in their original order, still makes the target fail. Shrinking matters: a 400-test prefix is not usable evidence in a review comment.

Run it against the failing target and the suite root:

Illustrative output on a suite where a new file landed ahead of an older one:

The predicate is order-preserving on purpose. You are not asking whether the two tests are related. You are asking whether this schedule is sufficient. Reordering the minimized subset afterwards is a separate and useful follow-up: if the pair fails in either order, you have shared global state, not a directional dependency.

Do not act on the bisection result until it lands in a row of this table.

Only row 3 earns a freeze. Rows 1 and 2 are test bugs with a named owner, and they cost a fixture edit rather than a suppression entry. Mixing the rows is how quarantine lists grow monotonically while suite reliability stays flat.

Whatever you conclude, write it next to the test. A suppression marker with no reason is an invitation for the next agent to "fix" it by deleting the test.

Two properties make this note useful: a named issue, and a stated removal condition. A freeze without an exit condition is a permanent deletion with extra steps.

The bisection is cheap per target but embarrassingly parallel across targets — every node ID in a failing run is a candidate root cause. That is a short-lived, bursty workload rather than a steady one, which is the shape a free server option handles well. It is why I ran this batch step on MonkeyCode's free server: the machine only needs to exist for the length of a triage pass, then it can go away.

The model side is the second half. Sorting a minimized prefix into the table above is a reading task — does the polluting test touch a session fixture, an env var, a module-level cache, a temp path? Drafting that first pass across dozens of prefixes is well within what free model access handles, and a human then confirms it by reading the two tests side by side. Treat the draft as a hypothesis generator, not a verdict.

Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach.

The gate is not "is this test flaky." The gate is "can I name the test that breaks it." Only one of those questions has an answer you can paste into a review comment.

#9733. This Vitamin Reduces Mental Health Problems By 50%

Around half the world’s population are thought to have an insufficiency of this vitamin.

Around half the world’s population are thought to have an insufficiency of this vitamin.

A triple dose of vitamin D3 supplementation in the first two years of life reduces the chance of mental health problems later on by around 50 percent, a high-quality experiment finds.

Infants who were given 30 µg of vitamin D daily, which is three times the recommended dose, were only half as likely to have internalising problems by age 6-8.

Internalising problems are those in which a person keeps their problems to themselves, including depression, anxiety, loneliness and withdrawal.

Dr Samuel Sandboge, the study’s first author, said:

“Our results suggest that a higher dose of vitamin D3 supplementation during the first years of life may reduce the risk of internalizing psychiatric symptoms in late preschool and early school age.”

The randomised controlled trial, which was carried out in Finland, was inspired by the link found between low childhood vitamin D levels and mental health problems.

Almost 350 children were given either a dose of 10 µg or 30 µg of vitamin D from age 2 weeks until 2-years-old.

The results showed that at 6- to 8-years-old, almost 12 percent of children given 10 µg had significant internalising problems.

In the 30 µg group, though, this figure was under 6 percent.

No differences were seen in the number of externalising problems.

Externalising disorders include ADHD and conduct disorder.

Later in life externalising disorders include substance abuse, antisocial personality disorders and even psychopathy.

Dr Samuel Sandboge warned that the study has drawbacks:

“The results and their potential implications are interesting, but further research is needed to confirm the results.

In the interpretation of the results, we must note, among other things, that we studied the psychiatric symptoms only as parent-reported.

Furthermore, the participants of the study were children with Nordic ancestry living in Finland who had good levels of vitamin D.”

Around half the world’s population are thought to have an insufficiency of vitamin D, and 10 percent are deficient.

Vitamin D plays an important role in the development of the brain.

It is notable that a rise in autism and ADHD rates has happened at a time when there have been significant drops in average levels of vitamin D.

The study was published in JAMA Network Open (Sandboge et al., 2023).

#9732. CWE-bench v2: More coverage, quality, and transparency

CWE-bench is designed to test the limits of frontier cyber capabilities. In our continued pursuit to push the horizon at Collinear AI, CWE-bench v2 opens up a public set of 100 tasks that anyone can run and evaluate their models on. The setup is the same as before. An agent gets a checkout of a real open-source repository and a short instruction, with the goal of finding and fixing a security weakness without breaking existing functionality. Scoring is fully programmatic, so results are deterministic and anyone can reproduce them without extra cost. All our programmatic checks have been curated with the help of LLM judge panels that shape them towards the direction of hardness and fairness. We also maintain a held-out set, so that we can keep tracking progress on tasks no model has seen. To evaluate your model on the held-out set, contact cyber@collinear.ai.

Our goal is to be exhaustive. A defender has to anticipate the ways an attacker could get in, and get it right every single time. These 100 tasks cover 91 different CWEs, spanning a wide range of vulnerability classes. A model that does well here has to understand the multiple weakness surfaces that a potential attacker can exploit. Recognising a familiar pattern is not enough.

As part of our meticulous effort to keep improving quality, for every task we checked that the following questions were true:

Every task was also reviewed by hand. Open-sourcing the set is part of the same effort to improve quality. We welcome feedback on any task, and contributions to the public set.

Results are tracked in two places on the Hub. The leaderboard on the CWE-bench dataset page covers open-weight models and updates on its own: labs and the community add a result by opening a PR on the model's repo with a results file (how). For the full comparison, including API-only models such as Gemini, Claude and GPT, see the CWE-bench leaderboard Space, where new models are added through a PR on the Space.

Open-weight models, from the dataset page:

All evaluated models, including API-only ones:

Of the 11 models evaluated, Gemini 4 Argon leads with 67.8% pass@1 and 81.0% pass@4, just ahead of Claude Opus 5.5 (67.3% pass@1, 78.0% pass@4). 95 tasks are solved by at least one model, an indication that the tasks are indeed solvable. However, even the leader fails 19% of the set on every attempt, so the long tail is far from solved. The public set, the grader and the harness are open. Run your model, and tell us where it stands.

On cost, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (1017), Claude Opus 5.5 and Gemini 4 Argon form the Pareto frontier: DeepSeek reaches 57.0% pass@1 at $0.04 per rollout, Opus adds ten points at $1.83, and Gemini edges ahead at $3.92.

Every task is a self-contained Harbor task (a Dockerized environment, an instruction, and a deterministic verifier), and the dataset ships a registry.json. Harbor can therefore run the whole benchmark straight from the Hugging Face repo, without cloning anything yourself:

-k 4 runs 4 attempts per task, and the reported score is the mean reward over all 400 trials. The dataset is gated: accept its access conditions on the dataset page first. Harbor fetches the tasks with git, so also save your HF token to git's credential helper once:

The tasks are also tagged rl-environment: the same environments and verifiers can provide rewards for training defensive agents, not just for evaluating them.

#9729. Your client paid you less than the invoice. Here's where the money went (and how to get it back)

If you freelance for companies in India, Indonesia, the Philippines, Spain, most of Latin America, parts of Africa, or you do construction work in the UK, you have probably had this moment: you invoice 2,000, and 1,800 lands in your account. No dispute, no late fee, no explanation.

The missing 200 is withholding tax (also called tax deducted at source, retención, PPh, TDS, CIS, or in the US "backup withholding"). Your client was legally required to keep part of your fee and pay it to the tax office in your name. It is not a cost — it is a prepayment of your own income tax. But it only counts as a prepayment if you can prove it. Most freelancers can't, so they pay the tax twice.

This post is the bookkeeping system I use to make sure that never happens, plus the spreadsheet logic so you can build it yourself.

The core mistake is tracking only the invoice total. Every invoice actually has three amounts you care about:

In a spreadsheet, with the fee in F, withholding rate in H and the sales-tax toggle in Settings:

Note the order: withholding is usually calculated on the pre-tax fee, and sales tax is added on top of it. If your country does it the other way, it's a one-cell change — but write the rule down once and apply it to every invoice, because a tracker that is inconsistent is worse than none.

Rates change. Clients also fall into categories (business with your tax ID on file, business without it, private individual, overseas). Put the categories and their rates in one small table and let every invoice look them up:

where column G is a dropdown of the type names. When your country's rate changes from 10% to 12%, you edit one cell and every invoice that uses that type updates. If you had typed 10% into 80 rows, you now have 80 edits and probably three mistakes.

A small discipline that pays off: keep NONE (0%) as the first row. Private clients and most overseas clients don't withhold, and "no type selected" should mean zero, not an error.

Here is what actually recovers the money. Your tax return lets you claim withheld tax as a credit, but the tax office will only accept it with the client's withholding certificate (Form 16A in India, bukti potong in Indonesia, CIS statement in the UK, etc.). Clients forget. You forget. By filing season it's a scramble.

So the tracker has one column on the invoice sheet — Certificate received? YES / NO / N/A — and a separate sheet that lists only the invoices with withholding, pulled automatically:

Then two numbers at the top of that sheet:

The second number is your to-do list. Chase it monthly, when the client's finance team still remembers the payment, not in April.

Now every dashboard number is a SUMIFS on those columns, with a <>CANCELLED guard so voided invoices never inflate revenue:

Twelve rows for months, four rows for quarters (sum of three months each), and you have: invoices issued, revenue, sales tax collected (this is your VAT return), tax withheld (this is your credit), net cash billed, cash received, outstanding. The quarterly block exists for estimated / advance tax payments, which most countries base on the quarter's actual income.

One more column I always add: suggested set-aside = cash received × a percentage you choose (I use 25%). It's not a tax computation, it's a nudge to move money into a separate account before it turns into a new lens.

A due date is just invoice date + terms. Days late depends on status:

Paid: how late was the payment. Unpaid: how late is it right now. Cancelled: zero. Add a conditional-format rule — red fill when P > 0 and status isn't PAID — and your receivables list reads itself. The dashboard KPIs then come free: overdue total, overdue count, average days to payment (AVERAGEIFS of P on paid invoices + terms), collection rate (cash received ÷ net cash billed).

You don't need an invoicing app for a clean invoice. One sheet, one yellow cell for the invoice number, and every field is:

Show subtotal, sales tax, total, then — and this is what clients appreciate — a line that says "Less tax withheld at source (WHT 10%): −200" and "Amount payable: 1,800". When the invoice already shows the net amount, nobody at the client's end has to guess, and you get far fewer "we paid what the invoice said" arguments.

That's the system: three amounts per invoice, rates in a lookup table, a certificate log, month/quarter helpers, status-aware lateness, and a print sheet. It takes about an evening to build from scratch.

If you'd rather not spend the evening, I packaged exactly this as a 7-sheet Excel workbook (5,700 live formulas, no macros, works in Excel / Google Sheets / LibreOffice, every rate is an input so it fits any country): Freelancer Invoice & Tax Tracker 2026 — English edition, $9. Indonesian freelancers: the bilingual edition with PPh 23 / PPh 21 / PPN pre-wired is here.

#9728. Palette: teaching a small model to build decks in your design language

Ask a frontier model for a slide deck and you'll get a good one. Ask for ten and they start to look alike: the same tasteful defaults, the same house style, a faint "AI-generated deck" look. That's fine until you want the deck to look like your template. Frontier models have their own house style, and no amount of prompting stops them drifting back to it. And sometimes the content is confidential and can't leave your systems at all.

Both of those point to a model you own: open weights, running on your own infrastructure, trained on your own design language. The catch is that small open models, the kind you'd actually self-host, are bad at this. Their decks come out broken: titles that vanish into the background, text running off the slide, shapes stacked on top of each other.

Palette tests one bet: that a small open-weight model, trained on synthetic data in your design language and checked by a harness, can compete with frontier systems while you keep ownership of the result. We fine-tuned a 20B model to build decks the way people do: a designer plans the deck and a coder draws each slide. Its training data follows the IBM Design Language, and on PresentBench it ranks first on two of the three domains we measured. This post covers how we synthesized the data, trained the model and built a harness around it.

A slide deck looks simple, but making one asks a model to do three things small models are bad at.

It lays out the slide without seeing it. The model doesn't draw slides; it writes code that places every element at an x, y, width and font size. Whether a 75-character title fits on two lines at 56pt is arithmetic the model does in its head, and it only finds out it was wrong after the code renders. Small models get this wrong often, which is where overlapping shapes and text running off the slide come from.

It makes two kinds of decisions at once. Deciding what each slide says and how to show it (a chart or a table? what to cut?) is editorial judgment. Placing it precisely is geometry. A single pass has to do both across 10–20 slides, while keeping the palette, type and layout consistent.

There's no data showing how decks get made. Plenty of finished decks exist, but not the rationale behind the design choices or the code that produced them.

Nobody makes a deck in one pass. You decide the story first (how many slides, what each one says, which gets a chart and which gets a table) and only then build each slide. Palette splits the work the same way, into two roles served by a single LoRA adapter:

Each role now makes one kind of decision: the designer handles the editorial judgment, and the coder handles the geometry. The brief between them is readable and editable, so a person or an agent can change one slide's layout without regenerating the deck. And because every slide's context is fixed before any code is written, the coder calls run in parallel, one per slide, which makes the coding stage about 6–7× faster.

We trained the adapter with LoRA rather than full fine-tuning: it teaches a format and a skill on top of a capable base without disturbing what the base already knows, and it made each experiment cheap. One lesson: coder examples are about 5× longer than designer examples, so a naive mix undertrained the designer until we oversampled its examples 5×.

There's no public corpus of plans, design decisions and slide code, so we generated one with a large open teacher. Each deck starts from a recipe that sets its genre, length, layouts and any user directives, so we control what the data covers. Plans range from tidy outlines to raw content dumps, so the model learns to cut and condense. We generated around 1000 decks covering roughly 10,000 slides.

Every example also carries the reasoning behind it, written as a counterfactual: the trace weighs an alternative and says why it was rejected, so the model learns the rule behind a choice, not just the choice. The designer reasons about content and form. For example:

"Revenue for four quarters, with one clear upward trend. I considered a table, but the point of this slide is the trend, not the exact figures, so a bar chart makes it visible at a glance."

"The title is 62 characters. At 44pt it would wrap to three lines and run into the chart below, so I set it at 36pt, which fits on two lines and leaves room above the chart."

The teacher alone doesn't make the data good; the loop around it does. Every synthesized deck is rendered and checked for overlaps and overflow by the same checker the harness uses at inference. Broken slides are repaired, and their reasoning is rewritten as the same kind of counterfactual, covering what the original layout got wrong and why the fix works. Each mistake the checker catches becomes a better training example.

The hardest problem was faithfulness. The worst failure is a slide with facts that weren't in the input, and we found that a prompt rule can't prevent it. If a brief asks for a six-by-five table but carries only three bullets, the coder has to invent the rest.

What fixed it was reference decks, not the rules: fixing a reference reliably changed the teacher's output, while adding a rule rarely did. The teacher sees a few reference decks in its prompt and copies them far more than it follows instructions.

Users often want finer-grained control over specific design choices: a chart instead of a table, a particular color, a darker cover. Palette lets them ask for these with directives, short instructions written directly in the plan and wrapped in [[ ]]:

The designer builds each directive into the brief, and the coder follows it when drawing the slide. Without the directive, the model would reasonably show these milestones as a table; with it, the model draws a timeline instead.

The model follows directives because it was trained to. The data recipes include directives from 12 categories, a few of which are shown below, each phrased several different ways, so the model learns the intent rather than a fixed phrase.

Figure 1. An illustration of the same plan without (left) and with (right) the [[make this a timeline]] directive.

Even a well-trained model sometimes produces a broken slide: a title in the same color as the background, or two boxes stacked on top of each other. So Palette doesn't return the model's output directly; every deck goes through a harness first.

Figure 2. The designer drafts the brief, the coder writes each slide's code in parallel, and the harness checks and repairs every slide before the deck is returned.

First, simple rules fix known mistakes, such as a malformed color code that would otherwise turn every slide black. Then each slide is rendered and measured: a geometry checker flags text that overlaps, gets clipped or runs off the slide. Flagged slides go to a separate editor model, which rewrites that slide's code.

The key rule is that a rewrite is kept only if the checker confirms the slide improved; otherwise the original stays. That makes the harness safe to run on every deck. It can fix a slide, but it can't make one worse.

Figure 3. An illustration of a repair. As generated (left), each card's title is stacked on top of its description; the harness detects the overlaps and reflows the cards into a 2×2 grid (right).

To measure its effect, we generated each PresentBench deck once and scored it with and without the harness. Across 131 decks, the harness adds 3.5 points on average.

We evaluate on PresentBench, which scores generated decks on five criteria: fundamentals, visual design, completeness, correctness and fidelity. PresentBench provides a source document rather than a plan, so for these runs a separate frontier model drafted each plan from its document, and Palette built the deck from that plan. We report three domains; baseline numbers are from the PresentBench paper.

Figure 4. PresentBench scores by domain. Palette (blue) against NotebookLM, Manus 1.6 and five other systems (gray). Palette ranks first on Economics and Education, third on Talk, and second on the three-domain mean.

Palette does best where structured content and numeric accuracy decide the score, ranking first on Economics and Education. On Talk, where decks are narrative and speech-driven, two closed systems score higher and Palette places third. Across the three domains it places second, 1.1 points behind NotebookLM (59.7 vs 60.8) and ahead of the rest of the field, as a single 20B open-weight model.

PresentBench measures whether a deck is good, but not whether it follows a specific design language. We're not aware of a benchmark that does, and it's a gap we hope to help close.

The harness already computes cheap, verifiable signals: does the slide render, does anything overlap or overflow, does every fact trace back to the brief. Today we use them to repair output after generation. Next, we want to use the same checks as rewards for reinforcement learning, so the model stops making these mistakes in the first place. Because the coder works one slide at a time, each slide is a short, independently checkable rollout, a natural fit for GRPO-style training.

We also want to close the gap on figure-heavy decks by extracting figures from source documents (e.g. with Docling) and placing them with the harness. And we're exploring a lighter way to bring your own templates: re-skinning output from one or two of your existing .pptx files, without retraining.

Building Palette taught us a few effective methods that extend naturally to other tasks whose output has a structure you can check in code, from charts and diagrams to UI layouts:

#9727. Most Frequently Asked Questions About NFTs(Non-Fungible Tokens)

Non-fungible tokens (NFTs) are the most popular digital assets today, capturing the attention of cryptocurrency investors, whales and people from around the world. People find it amazing that some users spend thousands or millions of dollars on a single NFT-based image of a monkey or other token, but you can simply take a screenshot for free. So here we share some freuently asked question about NFTs.

NFT stands for non-fungible  token, which is a cryptographic token on a blockchain with unique identification codes that distinguish it from other tokens. NFTs are unique and not interchangeable, which means no two NFTs are the same. NFTs can be a unique artwork, GIF, Images, videos, Audio album. in-game items, collectibles etc.

A blockchain is a distributed digital ledger that allows for the secure storage of data. By recording any kind of information—such as bank account transactions, the ownership of Non-Fungible Tokens (NFTs), or Decentralized Finance (DeFi) smart contracts—in one place, and distributing it to many different computers, blockchains ensure that data can’t be manipulated without everyone in the system being aware.

The value of an NFT comes from its ability to be traded freely and securely on the blockchain, which is not possible with other current digital ownership solutionsThe NFT points to its location on the blockchain, but doesn’t necessarily contain the digital property. For example, if you replace one bitcoin with another, you will still have the same thing. If you buy a non-fungible item, such as a movie ticket, it is impossible to replace it with any other movie ticket because each ticket is unique to a specific time and place.

One of the unique characteristics of non-fungible tokens (NFTs) is that they can be tokenised to create a digital certificate of ownership that can be bought, sold and traded on the blockchain.

As with crypto-currency, records of who owns what are stored on a ledger that is maintained by thousands of computers around the world. These records can’t be forged because the whole system operates on an open-source network.

NFTs also contain smart contracts—small computer programs that run on the blockchain—that give the artist, for example, a cut of any future sale of the token.

#9725. Draft Only What a Probe Can Fail: A Section Ownership Ledger for Model-Written Docs

Split documentation at the point where a claim can be falsified by a command. Everything on the machine-checkable side of that line may be drafted by a model; everything on the other side needs a named human author, not a reviewer. This post turns that rule into two small scripts and a tab-separated ledger you can run in CI.

Most doc-generation failures I have seen are not hallucinated sentences. They are correctly written sentences about a surface that changed, sitting in a section nobody was assigned to own. A reviewer checkbox does not fix that, because reviewing prose is cheap and owning a fact is expensive. The ledger makes the ownership explicit and makes the split mechanical.

A section is model-draftable only when it satisfies three conditions at once. Its factual content must be extractable from a program (CLI help text, config schema, HTTP headers, exit codes). Every number in the drafted prose must appear in that extracted bundle. And it must carry zero unresolved judgment claims, meaning no sentence of the form "you should prefer X because Y".

Everything else is human-owned. That includes migration advice, security guarantees, deprecation rationale, performance expectations, and any statement about intent. Those sections are not reviewed by a human after drafting; they are written by a human and merely proofread by whoever is available.

The split is worth doing because the two failure modes have different costs. A stale flag table wastes a reader's afternoon. A wrong migration recommendation wastes a reader's week.

Create docplan.tsv next to your docs directory. Five columns, tab-separated, one row per section. The probe column points at a test file relative to the plan; handwritten_claims counts the judgment statements you already know the section needs.

The important column is handwritten_claims. It is a declaration that this section contains sentences no probe can produce, and it forces the row into the human bucket. If a section starts at 0 and later grows judgment content, the count changes and the gate re-files it.

The gate does not know whether the docs are true. It only enforces that the plan is coherent and that every model-drafted section has a probe file that actually exists. That is enough to catch the common failure where a section is marked model-draftable and the test was deleted six weeks ago.

Run it as python3 ownership_gate.py docplan.tsv. On the table above it prints sections=5 model=3 human=2 and exits zero. Rename a probe file and it exits one with a line-pointer and the missing path.

Each probe writes a JSON bundle of the facts it can observe. The model receives the bundle and nothing else as a source of numbers. Keeping the bundle plain text matters: it makes the input diffable, so a reviewer can see that the flag list shrank by two entries this week.

This is also where a hosted environment saves time. MonkeyCode's free model access and free server option are operator-supplied availability claims, and they are relevant here in a narrow way: the drafting loop and the probe pipeline can both run on a throwaway machine instead of on the laptop that holds your credentials.

Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach.

A model can produce a fluent section that cites a real fact bundle and still misattribute a number, for example by pairing a timeout value with the wrong endpoint. The audit is deliberately narrow: it checks only that every numeral in the drafted section appears somewhere in that section's bundle. It cannot catch misattribution, which is why step 5 exists.

Call it per section: python3 fact_audit.py .docfacts/probe_cli.json docs/cli-flags.md. The exit code is the gate. A section that reports unbacked=0 is not correct; it is merely anchored.

Use this table when you are unsure which side of the line a section belongs on. The right column is not a review duty; it is authorship.

The most useful behaviour of this pipeline is that it does not fill the judgment sections. The generator writes stubs/migration-guide.md containing the four declared claims as open questions and the owning handle, and CI fails while those files are missing. The model never touches them, which removes the temptation to accept a plausible paragraph because it arrived on time.

That is the whole discipline: the model is fast where a test can disagree with it, and silent where only a person can.

Probe existence is not probe quality, so a probe that always emits an empty bundle will pass the gate and produce hollow docs. The numeric audit catches invented figures and nothing else, meaning wrong pairings of real facts survive it. The ledger also cannot verify that the named owner read anything, so treat the handle as an accountability statement rather than proof of work.

Finally, do not wire a free tier into a release-blocking path as a permanent assumption. Availability, model behaviour, and limits can change without notice; keep a fallback where the three machine sections are generated from the fact bundle by a local template when the drafting step is unavailable.

Skip the ledger if your documentation is primarily positioning, tutorials, or narrative explanation, because almost every section lands in the human bucket and the plan becomes paperwork. Skip it if your repository has no executable surface to probe, or if the docs change less often than the ledger itself would. Teams of one or two may also find the tab-separated file heavier than a single OWNERS note in the README.

If you want to try it, the two scripts above are the entire dependency list; start by classifying five existing sections and see how many survive as model-draftable.

#9723. StateBench: Testing how language models track state changes over long documents

We’re introducing StateBench, a benchmark for long-context state tracking—how well language models keep track of information about entities in long documents as they evolve.

State tracking underlies tasks from reading code, where variables are assigned and reassigned, to following a story as characters physically move around and objects change hands. For example, if a mystery novel states that “John gave Mary the knife” right before a murder occurs, it’s important to know that the state of each character has changed. However, not all state-tracking problems are created equal: some require only finding the latest update; harder ones require following a chain of changes, where one missed step can throw off the final answer. For example, a harder variant of our mystery state tracking would be if John gave Mary the item in his backpack, with it previously known that Edward put a knife in John’s backpack.

Transformers have well-documented theoretical limits on hard variants of state tracking with long dependency chains, helping motivate recurrent and hybrid architectures such as Gated DeltaNet that carry a running memory forward. Existing state-tracking tests tend to focus on the hardest cases, but as these designs become more common, researchers need to know which kinds of state tracking each architecture can handle. We would like to understand the differences between architectures not just on the hardest kinds of state tracking, but also on the simpler, potentially more common kinds.

To this end, we developed the StateBench benchmark to capture state-tracking problems of different complexity, which we used to evaluate the differences between language models with different architectures. We find that recurrent and hybrid models can generalize much farther than transformers when trained directly on these tasks, while frontier models including Gemini 3.8 Flash, Claude Opus 5.5, and GPT-6 Sol and Luna still break down on harder forms of state tracking as inputs grow longer.

StateBench consists of four difficulty levels that permit increasingly complex state update operations. For programmers, these levels of state tracking complexity can be understood as allowing different types of variable assignment operations:

These levels can be intuitively understood in terms of variable assignments, but they also represent theoretically motivated distinctions in state tracking rooted in Krohn–Rhodes theory, a branch of algebra that describes how state-tracking problems – which can be viewed as word problems over finite monoids – can be decomposed into atomic primitives. Each level in our hierarchy corresponds to a class of state-tracking problems that can be built out of a different set of primitives.

To compare the four levels fairly, we start with a general finite sequence of variable assignments and derive three easier versions from it, producing four comparable StateBench problems—one at each difficulty level. All four use the same number of variables and distinct values, with assignments appearing at the same points in the sequence; only the type of assignment changes.

We tested a range of open pretrained models on the r-trivial, aperiodic, and general finite levels of StateBench to see where their state tracking breaks down, and whether different architectures fail where theory predicts. Under standard theoretical assumptions, transformers can handle r-trivial robustly (and soluble and aperiodic to some degree) but are predicted to fail on general problems. In contrast, Gated DeltaNet with a more flexible memory update can, in principle, handle all four levels.

We started with open pretrained models, where the training data and context lengths are fully documented. These included two 7-billion-parameter models, Olmo 3 (a transformer) and Olmo Hybrid (which adds Gated DeltaNet layers), along with smaller models with 275 million and 2.7 billion parameters. All of these models were pretrained on the same data; none had seen contexts longer than 64,000 tokens during training, and we tested most of them on inputs well beyond that length.

When we scored each model, almost all performed well on r-trivial problems, lost accuracy on aperiodic ones as inputs grew, and stayed at chance on general finite problems. Problem format mattered here—the 275-million-parameter hybrid and Gated DeltaNet models scored near the ceiling on RULER-style r-trivial problems but were near chance on the same problems framed as spreadsheet edits. That gap is one reason StateBench tests the same underlying problem in several formats.

We then tested four frontier models – Gemini 3.8 Flash, Claude Opus 5.5, and GPT-6 Sol and Luna – asking them to read each sequence of variable assignments and generate the final value of every variable.

All four performed well on r-trivial and aperiodic problems. But on soluble and general finite problems, accuracy fell sharply as inputs grew longer, dropping to 13% or lower on the longest general finite problems. One likely factor is sensitivity; at these harder levels, many more steps can affect the final answer, leaving less room for a model to miss an update without getting the result wrong.

Next, we investigated whether models’ difficulty with the harder levels reflects limits of the architectures themselves, or whether pretraining simply doesn’t teach models to solve them. Targeted direct training is a more favorable setting that reveals to what degree state-tracking issues come from the underlying architecture and optimizer rather than the data used to pretrain a model.

We trained several 275-million-parameter models from scratch on StateBench: two transformer variants, two hybrids, and two Gated DeltaNet variants with different memory-update constraints. The models trained on sequences of up to 256 assignments and were tested on sequences as long as 64,000 assignments, or 250 times the maximum training length.

The architectures began to diverge as sequences grew longer. Gated DeltaNet and hybrid models generalized almost perfectly on r-trivial, aperiodic, and soluble problems out to the longest sequences we tested, tens of thousands of assignments. Transformers learned the easier levels but degraded on longer sequences, and they never learned general finite problems. On the hardest level, the Gated DeltaNet variant with a more flexible memory update generalized the farthest, staying near perfect out to roughly 10 times the length of the longest sequences it saw during training.

For Gated DeltaNet and hybrid models, the gap points to training rather than architecture; trained directly, they learned to handle state-tracking levels their pretrained counterparts couldn’t. Transformers were different—even trained directly, they could never learn the hardest level.

Some questions remain open. Our new proof shows that Gated DeltaNet with a more limited memory update (non-negative eigenvalues) can solve all aperiodic tasks and certain periodic tasks, such as tracking whether a repeated input has occurred an even or odd number of times, under the paper’s fixed-precision arithmetic with rounding. Its exact placement in the hierarchy remains open, including whether it can solve all soluble tasks and how numerical precision or combining it with attention layers affects its capabilities. StateBench also assumes a fixed number of variables, while real tasks often introduce new entities over time. In a long conversation, for example, new people and objects can appear as it unfolds, and the model has to begin tracking them too. The current framework doesn’t yet cover that setting.

As new flavors of recurrent and hybrid architectures emerge, understanding which kinds of state tracking each can handle could help guide how future systems are developed and trained. We hope StateBench gives researchers a finer-grained way to find where models break down—and to build training and evaluation data for the capabilities that still fall short. More fundamentally, we hope it serves as a North Star for researchers to develop new architectures with more robust state-tracking abilities compared to current models.

#9722. 6 of the Best Company Enrichment APIs in 2026 (A Benchmark-Based Comparison)

Access real-time exclusive B2B data APIs that power your platforms, AI agents, workflows, and GTM operations.

Access real-time exclusive B2B data APIs that power your platforms, AI agents, workflows, and GTM operations.

Access real-time exclusive B2B data APIs that power your platforms, AI agents, workflows, and GTM operations.

A practical guide to coverage, missing fields, matching behavior, and choosing an API for the product you are building.

A company enrichment API can return a profile and still leave your application missing the information it needs. In our six-provider comparison, CompanyEnrich led overall coverage and profile depth, while competitors led individual fields. That makes the required fields in your workflow a useful place to start choosing an API.

Enrichment looks simple in a demo. Send a domain. Get a company profile. Add the fields to your application.

The more useful question comes after the response arrives: can your application actually use it?

A lead-routing workflow might need employee count and headquarters country. A market-mapping product might need corporate relationships. An account research agent might need a description and reliable company identifiers. Those applications can reach different conclusions about the same response.

We recommend choosing a company enrichment API by starting with the fields and decisions it needs to support. A large response is helpful only when it contains the information your workflow requires.

Here is what our six-provider comparison can tell you, where its limits are, and how to turn the results into a shortlist.

This comparison uses CompanyEnrich’s published benchmark. The evaluation began with 500 selected domains from the Majestic Million; 349 passed the DNS check and became the benchmark set.

The sampling code and methodology narrow that description: selection was restricted to alphabetic root .com domains and balanced across prefixes. These were not 349 manually verified businesses or a representative sample of every market.

Field presence does not establish accuracy. The study did not manually verify every company match or returned value, and it does not rank production latency or price.

The normalization measures presence rather than equal detail: a location can be a country alone, and funding can be any mapped funding signal.

Source: the published benchmark report, checked October 13, 2026. Find rates and average profile depth are rounded to one decimal place. Profile-depth averages exclude unmatched domains.

For an integration, coverage and depth answer different questions. A provider can return fewer profiles while supplying more information on the ones it finds. You also need to check which information is present: an extra social link cannot fill a missing employee-count requirement.

The order below follows the published find rate. Field-level observations also draw on the published comparison. The evaluation priorities are our recommendations; your own accounts and required fields should determine the final choice.

CompanyEnrich led the published comparison on find rate and average profile depth. That makes it a reasonable starting point when an application needs several company attributes from a domain lookup.

It did not lead every field. Employee-count or range presence was 50.4% for CompanyEnrich versus 60.2% for People Data Labs, which matters if that field drives your qualification rules.

Its domain-enrichment documentation describes a useful implementation choice: waitForEnrichment=false returns stored data immediately. If the company is not stored, the API returns a 404, schedules enrichment in the background, and does not charge for that response.

That behavior matters for a signup flow. You can let the user continue and arrange a later lookup instead of making account creation depend on enrichment finishing. Your application needs to distinguish that condition from other failures and use bounded retries.

Evaluate it for company profiles, account qualification, and other workflows that use several fields together. Check the exact required fields before treating a returned profile as a successful outcome.

Apollo is worth evaluating when enrichment needs to fit an existing sales workflow. Its organization-enrichment endpoint supports company identifiers including domain, LinkedIn URL, and website; a name can help improve matching. Returned data can include industry, employee counts, revenue, funding, and corporate relationships.

Apollo placed second in the published comparison. It also had slightly higher technology and funding-field presence than CompanyEnrich. Those are small observed differences, so we recommend testing the fields on your target accounts before using them to choose a provider.

During evaluation, confirm that your account and API key have the required access, and include enrichment credits in the cost model. Existing access can make an initial pilot easier; it does not settle the data-quality question.

People Data Labs deserves attention when matching controls and specific company fields drive the decision. In the comparison, it led LinkedIn URL coverage and corporate-relationship presence.

Its enrichment parameters expose min_likelihood, which sets the minimum match score, and required, which specifies fields a result must contain. Raising the matching threshold can reduce returned results while filtering weaker matches.

That is a useful tradeoff to make explicit. A workflow that automatically updates customer records may value a stricter match more than a larger number of responses.

Record these settings in any comparison you run. Otherwise, different matching thresholds can make provider coverage numbers difficult to interpret.

ContactOut is worth including when company enrichment sits alongside contact-data workflows. Its company endpoint accepts domains and returns company information. The documentation shows that a successful HTTP response can contain an empty companies array, so your client must inspect the result before recording a match.

The comparison showed a narrower overall profile but useful strengths: ContactOut led follower-count presence and shared the highest revenue-field presence with Crustdata.

Those fields may justify a trial for a particular application. They do not establish that the revenue estimates are correct or that follower count predicts buying intent.

Check what each field represents, how often it is populated for your accounts, and whether its definition fits your scoring model.

Coresignal is worth testing when enrichment feeds company and workforce analysis. Its company-enrichment endpoint accepts website URLs and supports selecting data bundles and fields.

In the comparison, Coresignal returned fewer profiles than People Data Labs and ContactOut, but its matched profiles had a higher average field count. That is a useful reminder to inspect both dimensions of the table.

There is a practical constraint: selected fields must belong to the requested bundles, or the API returns an error. Record the product, endpoint, and bundle configuration in your test; the benchmark is a dated snapshot of the tested configuration.

Start with the fields your application needs, map their definitions, and then measure coverage against those requirements.

Crustdata is worth evaluating when company profiles need headcount, funding, hiring, or other selected data groups. Its enrichment API returns basic information by default; request the other groups explicitly. Responses can also contain multiple candidate companies, which your application must resolve.

That request configuration belongs in your evaluation notes. Comparing one provider’s default response with another provider’s expanded response can change the apparent winner before you inspect any data.

When several candidate records share a domain, apply your own entity-selection rules before using their headcount or funding data in an automated workflow.

Suppose you are building inbound lead routing. You decide that a record is usable only when it has the correct company identity, a headquarters country, and an employee-size field your routing rules understand.

Write that requirement down before comparing vendors. A profile with twenty other fields still cannot route the lead if a required value is missing.

Keep three measurements separate: profiles returned, profiles with all required fields, and profiles whose identity and important values pass your review. Each stage can remove records from the previous one.

Build a pilot from your actual market. Include smaller companies, different geographies, redirects, and ambiguous brand names where they occur in your workload. Keep the input set identical across providers.

A few hundred domains can help expose integration problems and obvious coverage gaps. It will not establish the error rate for every segment. For a large purchase, expand the sample and report results by the segments that matter to the product.

Review whether a result describes the company you intended, its parent, a subsidiary, or another business with a similar name.

Then inspect the fields your application uses. Employee ranges and employee counts may require different routing logic. Headquarters location and operating locations answer different questions. A revenue estimate should not silently become reported revenue in your database.

Preserve source and retrieval metadata where available, and decide how to handle disagreements before allowing enrichment to overwrite existing records.

Use a denominator that reflects the outcome you need:

Cost per usable record = total evaluation spend / records meeting your acceptance criteria

Include the subscription or minimum commitment allocated to the workload, credits, retries, and any separately charged fields. Measure response-time percentiles and timeouts alongside cost if enrichment runs in a user-facing flow.

If you add a second provider, measure how many additional usable records it supplies after the first provider fails. Its standalone coverage does not tell you how much it will improve your waterfall.

Start by shortlisting providers whose documented interfaces and field definitions fit your application, then run the same acceptance test against each.

The benchmark helps identify candidates. The production decision comes from the overlap between correct company matches, required fields, acceptable latency, and sustainable cost.

Before making the first request, finish this sentence: “An enriched company record is useful to us only when it contains…”

The answer gives you a much better test than counting every key in the JSON.

#9721. Paper 5: What survives when the model, client, and machine change?

A model session ending should not mean that the system forgets who is authorized, what is in scope, what evidence supports a record, or how an earlier decision can be audited.

That sounds obvious—until you ask where those things actually live.

If they live only in a live prompt, a model’s context window, a particular client, or the memory of one running process, then they are not really system continuity. They are temporary convenience.

My fifth preprint, The Continuity Substrate, tests a different proposition: can governed operational continuity survive changes in models, clients, machines, operating systems, and runtime restarts when the continuity contract is maintained outside the inference session?

The answer from this controlled study is narrow but encouraging.

Under named first-party synthetic conditions, the governed substrate preserved its deterministic contract across:

The point is not that any model has become magically permanent. It has not.

The point is that important continuity should not be entrusted to a model session in the first place.

In this architecture, models can change. Clients can change. A runtime can restart. The intelligence can come and go. What must remain stable—authority, scope, provenance, consent, auditability, and the rules for releasing information—belongs in a governed substrate outside inference.

That matters for ordinary software as much as it matters for AI. If someone changes providers, upgrades a model, moves from one device to another, or restarts a service, they should not have to negotiate their digital history from scratch. And they should never discover that a new model has quietly inherited information it was not authorized to see.

There are real limits to this paper. It does not claim production readiness, security certification, universal portability, or independent replication. It reports a controlled test and a public evidence package so readers can inspect the boundary being claimed.

But it asks a question I think the industry needs to take more seriously:

When the intelligence changes, where does the responsibility stay?

Read the open preprint and inspect the public evidence package here:

The model may be brilliant. But continuity, permission, and accountability should not disappear when the model closes its eyes.
