#9719. Dharma Field Extractor: Any Document In, Structured Fields in JSON Out

A 2-billion-parameter model that extracts exactly the fields you ask for, from any document type, outperforming every frontier LLM we tested, at a fraction of the cost.

In April, we released DharmaOCR-LITE, a model specialized for OCR across a wide range of documents, from contracts and court filings to invoices, IDs and forms. The paper behind it made a narrow, well-measured case for domain specialization: a smaller model trained closer to its task beating general-purpose frontier APIs on that task.

OCR gives you the text on a page, faithful to the original formatting. That's exactly what you want when the job is the whole document, like a contract you'll read end to end or a manuscript you're digitizing.

However, there's a different use case: you don't want the page, you want specific fields out of it, in a shape a system downstream can consume. Every line item on an invoice, as a list. The patient name, exam type and date from a medical requisition, ready to schedule. The fields off an ID, mapped to the columns of an employee record.

Run that document through OCR and you get back everything printed on it, line by line, with no indication of which string is the exam type, which is the date or which number is the total. Someone still has to write the code that maps each value to the right field before it reaches the database.

A general-purpose LLM can do this work today, with careful prompting. At frontier API pricing and latency, on a task many businesses need to run at high volume, that quickly becomes the expensive way to solve a well-defined problem.

So we built a model for it instead. The Field Extractor takes a document image and either a request for everything it can find, or an exact schema to fill, and returns structured JSON: typed, field by field, nested where the document nests. An invoice comes back with every line item as an ordered list, each with its own quantity and value, alongside the totals. An ID comes back as the fields you'll store, under the names your system already uses for them. The same checkpoint handles all of it, with no per-type fine-tuning.

Say a batch of supplier invoices lands every morning, and you need four things off each one to push into your system: the supplier, the invoice number, the due date, the total. Same story for medical requisitions going into a scheduler, or contracts feeding a compliance system, where what matters is the parties, the term, the penalties and the fine amounts. You don't need the page, you need certain fields. With the Field Extractor there are two ways to ask for them:

The choice comes down to what you already know. Send an open request when you don't know what the document holds. Send a schema when the output has to match a shape that already exists somewhere else.

Either way, what comes back is JSON: the fields as keys, the values typed as requested, and null where the document didn't have what you asked for. When you send a schema, the output follows it exactly, with the same keys and no extra fields, so it can go straight into the next system.

The base model is DharmaOCR-LITE v1.1, a new 2-billion-parameter version optimized from the one in the paper and already specialized for OCR through supervised fine-tuning and DPO. On top of that checkpoint we trained a LoRA adapter on 43,384 training examples covering both request modes.

The data is organized into three streams:

All three streams are annotated at the field level. The mix is deliberately multi-domain: receipts, commercial invoices, forms, bank statements, ID documents and synthetic documents, rather than one filing type.

The full benchmark covers 546 documents across three request scenarios, for 1,638 total cases: extracting every field with no schema, a partial schema naming only real fields, and a schema that also includes deliberately nonexistent fields. The score is field-level F1 (matched by path, including position inside a table), multiplied by the Levenshtein similarity on the values that matched and by the share of outputs that come back as valid JSON.

We ran the same benchmark against four general-purpose frontier configurations.

Against general-purpose LLMs, the quality gap runs from 1.8 points (Claude Opus 5, the closest) to 9.3 points (GPT-5.6 Luna, the widest).

Cost runs from roughly 6 times lower (GPT-5.6 Luna) to roughly 147 times lower (GPT-5.6 Sol). The two sides are priced differently. The frontier figures come from measured average input and output tokens per page, reasoning tokens included, against each provider's published list pricing. Every frontier model ran with reasoning set to low; Claude Opus 5 used adaptive effort, which can skip reasoning on simpler pages while staying at the low level. Ours isn't billed per token: the model runs self-hosted, so the figure is GPU time on a single L40S at $2.24 per hour.

This is not a sales price. Self-hosted cost depends on the hardware, the volume and the latency each deployment needs. The comparison is here to show that a sovereign SSLM, deployed on your own infrastructure, is a real alternative to frontier APIs.

SROIE and FUNSD are two public datasets in our benchmark, not used in training. Below is one example from each.

On a SROIE receipt, we asked for all 18 fields printed on it, with no phantom fields this time, and every one comes back correct: the multi-line, unlabeled billing address captured as a single field, the two blank fields (salesperson and ref) correctly returned as null, and every number on the receipt matching to the cent.

On a FUNSD photocopying variance form, a checklist of twelve boolean fields with one nested group of five sub-options, the model marks exactly the one box that's checked (poor quality original, with a handwritten "faded" note beside it) as true, and the other eleven as false, matching the form exactly. It also reads the handwritten Bates ID off the page correctly, and returns null for the two fields left blank.

A 2-billion-parameter model scored 0.834, above every frontier configuration we tested, from Claude Opus 5 at 0.816 to GPT-5.6 Luna at 0.741, while running on a single L40S at a lower cost per extraction than every API in the comparison. Higher quality and lower cost, measured on the same benchmark, in the same run.

This isn't the first time we've measured it. Our OCR paper put the first DharmaOCR-LITE, a 3-billion-parameter model, above every commercial frontier API tested on Brazilian Portuguese; three months later, newer and better-resourced models arrived, and the gap held. Now a 2-billion-parameter model does it on field extraction. Each result adds evidence for the thesis we started Dharma-AI with: on a bounded task, a small model trained close to that task beats a frontier model asked to do the same thing in general. In this benchmark, it also cost 6 to 147 times less to run.

Parameter count sets the ceiling; training decides how much of it a model reaches on your task. Your business doesn't need the biggest model available. It needs one trained for your problem.

Try it on your own documents here. To learn more about Dharma-AI and the specialized models we build, visit dharma-ai.com.

#9718. A Passing Characterization Test Proves Nothing Until You Break the Code

Most characterization tests in a messy repo are decoration. They pass before the refactor. They pass after it. They would also pass if the branch under test were deleted.

That is not a test. It is a receipt. This post adds one cheap gate: prove each new test can fail, by breaking the code on purpose.

A vacuous test usually appears during refactor prep. Someone snapshots a return value. Or writes assert result is not None. It goes green, the team feels safe, and the gate stays open.

Then the refactor changes rounding, ordering, or a default. The suite stays green. The bug ships. The test was never guarding the seam you touched.

Coverage does not catch this. A line can execute and still be unobserved. The only honest question is: which code change makes this test fail?

Adopt a single rule for refactor prep. Every new characterization test must kill at least one deliberate mutation.

A mutation is a tiny, mechanical edit to the source. Change >= to > — swap a default — drop a rounding call. If the test still passes, the test cannot see that behavior.

Keep the mutant set small and hand-written. You are guarding a seam, not scoring the whole file.

Refactors fail at boundaries, not at file scope. Name the boundary before you write anything: a function, a public method, a serialized payload.

Write that name down. Also write the caller that must keep working. If you cannot name the caller, you are not ready to refactor.

Mutation results are worthless when the test is random. Pin time, IDs, and env reads behind module-level functions you can patch.

Run the target test five times in a row. If any run differs, stop. Fix determinism before you fix anything else.

Run the current code and record what it actually produces. Not what you believe it should produce. Paste that output into the assertion.

Ugly golden values are fine here. They are temporary scaffolding for the diff. You delete or re-derive them after the behavior is documented.

List the edits that would break a caller without crashing. Boundaries, defaults, rounding, and ordering are the usual suspects.

Keep them as data, not as a tool config. Two to six entries per seam is enough.

Each mutant must match exactly once. A pattern that matches zero or three times is a broken mutant, not a survived one.

The runner copies the repo, applies one mutant, runs one test node, then restores the file. Classify the exit code honestly.

Exit code 5 deserves attention. It means the selector matched no tests, which silently poisons the whole gate.

Survivors split into two kinds. Real gaps get a tighter assertion. Equivalent mutants — edits with no observable behavior change — should be deleted from the list, not chased.

Writing mutants by hand is fast. Finding the seams you forgot is not. A model is decent at proposing candidate assertions and candidate mutants for unfamiliar code.

Give it the function and the callers. Ask for boundary inputs and, for each input, the one-line edit that should change the output. Then run the loop.

The loop is the judge. A model proposal that kills nothing is dropped, no matter how plausible the reasoning sounds. Free model access on MonkeyCode is enough for this propose-then-verify pattern, since the artifact is text, not a passing test suite. The same loop runs fine on a remote machine; MonkeyCode's free server option is one place to park it if you would rather not pin a laptop core. Check the current quotas and limits yourself — free tiers change without notice.

Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach.

Now edit production code. One seam per commit. Then re-run the exact same mutant set.

The kill set must be identical before and after. New kills mean you changed behavior nobody asked for. Lost kills mean the test stopped guarding the seam.

That comparison is the gate. It is also cheaper than reviewing a large diff by eye.

Start with one module and one seam. Run the loop once. Count the survivors before you write any new test.

That count is your real starting point for the refactor.

#9717. How to Survive (Not Thrive) as a Salaryman

Every generation predicted the death of the middle manager. Every generation was wrong. Now AI is reorganizing firms toward the middle.

Every generation predicted the death of the middle manager. Every generation was wrong. Now AI is reorganizing firms toward the middle.

Every generation predicted the death of the middle manager. Every generation was wrong. Now AI is reorganizing firms toward the middle.

Fifteen rules for remaining employed, reasonably sane, and difficult to blame until the train takes you home.

The objective is not promotion. It is not fulfillment. It is not becoming indispensable.

The objective is to remain employed, reasonably sane, and difficult to blame until the train takes you home.

Arriving dramatically early creates expectations. Arriving late creates evidence.

Aim for the narrow zone in which everyone thinks, Yes, he was already here.

You do not necessarily need to work late. You need to understand who notices when you leave.

If your boss is putting on his coat, congratulations: you have suddenly remembered that you also own a coat.

A folder. A laptop. A notebook. Three pieces of paper.

A person walking quickly while carrying a document is almost universally presumed to have somewhere important to be.

The salaryman’s most efficient communication technology.

Someone explains a problem you don’t control: nod.

Someone announces an initiative that will disappear in six months: deeper nod.

Someone asks whether you understand: nod while saying, “Hai.”

Responsibility can theoretically produce promotion.

Blame can definitely produce unemployment.

When receiving an important instruction, create a polite written record of what was decided. You are not building a case against your coworkers. You are ensuring that six months from now nobody discovers that everyone remembers the meeting differently.

Being uniquely useful is also dangerous because nobody will ever let you go home.

The ideal salaryman occupies the fertile middle:

“It would be inconvenient if Tanaka weren’t here.”

A task that takes everyone three hours but takes you 45 minutes does not create 2 hours and 15 minutes of freedom.

You have discovered one of the fundamental laws of salaried employment.

You cannot defeat rain by becoming angry at clouds.

Attend. Take notes. Say one useful thing. Determine whether anything has actually been assigned to you.

The after-work drinking session is allegedly recreational and occasionally neither.

You don’t have to become the drunkest person in the izakaya. Eat. Participate. Pour drinks when appropriate. Laugh. Learn things.

Most importantly, recognize that the organizational chart becomes unusually honest after the second beer.

The train is not merely transportation. It is the membrane between Corporation You and Actual You.

Music. Manga. Games. Books. Staring into nothingness.

Do not voluntarily convert every commute into additional unpaid work.

A company capable of surviving earthquakes, recessions, executive reorganizations and forty-seven PowerPoint presentations can probably withstand your absence until Tuesday.

A family. Basketball. Gardening. Gundam models. A terrible band. Fishing. A neighborhood bar. An obsessive interest in 16th-century maps.

Anything that allows you to answer “Who are you?” without stating your employer.

Some years you acquire skills. Some years you make money. Some years you encounter an excellent boss. Some years you simply avoid the restructuring.

A 30-year career contains a surprising amount of successfully doing nothing catastrophic.

The presentation can be revised tomorrow.

If everything is always urgent, you are not experiencing urgency. You are experiencing management.

The old salaryman bargain was essentially:

Give us your loyalty and we will give you security.

Modern companies cannot always provide the second half.

If the company stops paying adequately, destroys your health, threatens your family life, or offers neither security nor opportunity, remaining loyal isn’t salaryman stoicism.

Show up.Be useful.Don’t become indispensable.Know who actually makes decisions.Keep receipts.Take the vacation.Catch the train.Go home.Have a life there.Repeat until retirement—or a better offer.

Answer the Salaryman Interview on HackerNoon: 27 questions about middle management, rituals, the company bargain, and AI agents. Your answers become a draft you can submit to HackerNoon for publication. Read the interviews, or explore more at salaryman.tech.

Originally published as Field Notes No. 1 on salaryman.tech.

Canva has a web version and also a mobile app

Canva is a free graphic design web application that allows you to create invitations, business cards, flyers, lesson plans, banners, and more using professionally designed templates. You can upload your own photos from your computer or from Google Drive, and add them to Canva's templates using a simple drag-and-drop interface. It's like having a basic version of Photoshop that doesn't require Graphic designing knowledge to use. It’s best for nongraphic designers.

Canva is a great tool for small business owners, online entrepreneurs, and marketers who don’t have the time and want to edit quickly.

To create sophisticated graphics, a tool such as Photoshop can is ideal. To use it, you’ll need to learn its hundreds of features, get familiar with the software, and it’s best to have a good background in design, too.

Also running the latest version of Photoshop you need a high-end computer.

So here  Canva takes place, with Canva you can do all that with drag-and-drop feature. It’s also easier to use and free. Also an even-more-affordable paid version is available for $12.95 per month.

The product is available in three plans: Free, Pro ($12.99/month per user or  $119.99/year for up to 5 people), and Enterprise ($30 per user per month, minimum 25 people).

To get started on Canva, you will need to create an account by providing your email address, Google, Facebook or Apple credentials. You will then choose your account type between student, teacher, small business, large company, non-profit, or personal. Based on your choice of account type, templates will be recommended to you.

You can sign up for a free trial of Canva Pro, or you can start with the free version to get a sense of whether it’s the right graphic design tool for your needs.

When you sign up for an account, Canva will suggest different post types to choose from. Based on the type of account you set up  you'll be able to see templates categorized by the following categories: social media posts, documents, presentations, marketing, events, ads, launch your business, build your online brand, etc.

Start by choosing a template for your post or searching for something more specific. Search by social network name to see a list of post types on each network.

Next, you can choose a template. Choose from hundreds of templates that are ready to go, with customizable photos, text, and other elements.

You can start your design by choosing from a variety of ready-made templates, searching for a template matching your needs, or working with a blank template.

Inside the Canva designer, the Elements tab gives you access to lines and shapes, graphics, photos, videos, audio, charts, photo frames, and photo grids.The search box on the Elements tab lets you search everything on Canva.

To begin with, Canva has a large library of elements to choose from. To find them, be specific in your search query. You may also want to search in the following tabs to see various elements separately:

The Photos tab lets you search for and choose from millions of professional stock photos for your templates.

You can replace the photos in our templates to create a new look. This can also make the template more suited to your industry.

You can find photos on other stock photography sites like pexel, pixabay and many more or simply upload your own photos.

When you choose an image, Canva’s photo editing features let you adjust the photo’s settings (brightness, contrast, saturation, etc.), crop, or animate it.

The Text tab lets you add headings, normal text, and graphical text to your design.

When you click on  text, you'll see options to adjust the font, font size, color, format, spacing, and text effects (like shadows).

Create an animated image or video by adding audio to capture user’s attention in social news feeds.

If you want to use audio from another stock site or your own audio tracks, you can upload them in the Uploads tab or from the more option.

Want to create your own videos? Choose from thousands of stock video clips. You’ll find videos that range upto 2 minutes

You can upload your own videos as well as videos from other stock sites in the Uploads tab.

Once you have chosen a video, you can use the editing features in Canva to trim the video, flip it, and adjust its transparency.

On the Background tab, you’ll find free stock photos to serve as backgrounds on your designs. Change out the background on a template to give it a more personal touch.

The Styles tab lets you quickly change the look and feel of your template with just a click. And if you have a Canva Pro subscription, you can upload your brand’s custom colors and fonts to ensure designs stay on brand.

If you have a Canva Pro subscription, you’ll have a Logos tab. Here, you can upload variations of your brand logo to use throughout your designs.

With Canva, you can also create your own logos. Note that you cannot trademark a logo with stock content in it.

With Canva, free users can download and share designs to multiple platforms including Instagram, Facebook, Twitter, LinkedIn, Pinterest, Slack and Tumblr.

Canva Pro allows you to work with your team on visual content. Designs can be created inside Canva, and then sent to your team members for approval. Everyone can make comments, edits, revisions, and keep track via the version history.

When it comes to printing your designs, Canva has you covered. With an extensive selection of printing options, they can turn your designs into anything from banners and wall art to mugs and t-shirts.

Canva Print is perfect for any business seeking to make a lasting impression. Create inspiring designs people will want to wear, keep, and share. Hand out custom business cards that leave a lasting impression on customers' minds.

The Canva app is available on the Apple App Store and Google Play. The Canva app has earned a 4.9 out of five star rating from over 946.3K Apple users and a 4.5 out of five star rating from over 6,996,708 Google users.

In addition to mobile apps, you can use Canva’s integration with other Internet services to add images and text from sources like Google Maps, Emojis, photos from Google Drive and Dropbox, YouTube videos, Flickr photos, Bitmojis, and other popular visual content elements.

In general, Canva is an excellent tool for those who need simple images for projects. If you are a graphic designer with experience, you will find Canva’s platform lacking in customization and advanced features – particularly vectors. But if you have little design experience, you will find Canva easier to use than advanced graphic design tools like Adobe Photoshop or Illustrator for most projects. #9715. A Closer Look at Phonon TTS. Launching High-Quality On-Device Speech That Tops the Benchmarks.

Two weeks ago, we opened up Phonon, our small text-to-speech model that runs on your own device. It needs no server and no network, and what you type stays with you.

We've been very happy with the reception so far. So here's the story of the launch: why we built Phonon, what it can do, the demos that came with it, and how it did on Hugging Face's Open TTS Leaderboard.

Most voice AI lives in the cloud: every sentence makes a round trip to a server. Phonon runs on your own device instead. Your text stays there and the voice works without a network. We’ve also opened the weights. Phonon 31m is Apache 2.0, so you can use it for free, even in a commercial product. The other models are CC BY-NC, so they’re free for non-commercial projects. If you’re building something commercial with those, pricing is based on your number of users, not how much speech you generate.

Getting a good voice to run on a small device has always been hard. You could make the model small, but then it didn’t sound great. Or you could make it sound great, but then it wouldn’t fit. We addressed both.

We announced Phonon in April and spent the next six months building on it with partners and early users. Their feedback helped us to shape this release. The models got smaller, and we added more languages and support for custom voices through voice cloning and voice design.

Phonon is based on the Pocket TTS lineage and as such uses flow matching to generate the audio which is very different from the modeling techniques used in other TTS systems. This is what allowed us to bring this level of quality to such a small model but it created new challenges while training the models. The training was initially numerically unstable and required several tricks to produce quality results on all five languages.

Phonon comes in two sizes, at about 65 MB and 75 MB. Together they speak English, French, German, Spanish and Portuguese. There are more than 100 built-in voices, and you can create your own in Gradium Studio. Phonon also handles the important things that most other TTS systems often stumble on, like phone numbers, dates and codes.

It runs on phones, laptops, single-board computers and in a browser tab, so you can hear it right now. Phonon 31m speaks English and is Apache 2.0, so you can build on it freely, including for commercial products. Phonon 40m covers all five languages under a non-commercial license.

The launch came with demos from friends and from our own team. On an Apple Watch with Wi-Fi off, Phonon talks you through a coffee brew step by step. On an iPhone with no signal, it counts your reps and keeps you going. A robot called Lamp, from Autonomous, wears a sorting hat and talks in character. In a browser, an offline dino runner becomes a radio show hosted by Rex. There's also a sci-fi game voiced on the player's own machine, and Proust read aloud page by page.

The Hugging Face team built the Transformers integration, so developers could use Phonon in Transformers from day one.

Developers have started building on it too. An ExecuTorch conversion runs Phonon on a visitor's GPU in the browser, Micdrop brings it to Node.js apps, and Spaces like smallest-s2s build on it.

Phonon was downloaded more than 200,000 times in its first two weeks, and it’s still trending on Hugging Face.

The Open TTS Leaderboard is a very new project from Hugging Face, and we love it. With more than 9,000 TTS models on the Hugging Face Hub, the leaderboard gives developers one place to compare open models and hear them side by side. Across 23 languages, models are evaluated on intelligibility (word error rate of the outputs), speed (inverse real-time factor and time-to-first audio), and naturalness (UTMOS for English and KOMOS for Korean). Fixed-voice and voice cloning are evaluated, with an additional speaker similarity metric for the latter. The leaderboard also has a Listen tab, where you can conveniently compare TTS outputs yourself and vote for the ones you like the most.

On intelligibility, Phonon ranks first in German and Spanish, and in the top three in every language we evaluated, next to models up to 100 times its size.

Speed is where we see Phonon truly shine, as the models top the CPU streaming benchmark on time-to-first audio.

We built a new inference framework, ptts, specifically for Phonon. The goal of ptts is to get the best performance on a wide variety of devices and as such supports more than 10 backends: CPU (Intel, Arm, WebAssembly), GPU (CUDA, Vulkan, Metal, WebGPU), and NPU (Apple Core ML, Snapdragon®).

Phonon is also available in 🤗 Transformers, from v5.21, as its reference PyTorch implementation. Where ptts runs a single stream on device, Transformers targets GPU throughput: batched generation, full-graph torch.compile, e.g., for synthesizing speech datasets at scale. Being native PyTorch, it is a base to build upon, whether to integrate Phonon into your own stack or to study the model itself.

It belongs to the Pocket TTS lineage, so we first added Pocket TTS to Transformers. Phonon sits on top as a modular model: about 200 lines describing only what differs.

Phonon generates audio latents autoregressively: each step outputs a latent that is fed back as the next input, and the training loss is computed on them. Latents are the model's inputs, outputs and targets, as text tokens are for a language model, so the codec mapping audio to latents plays the role of a tokenizer. Transformers ships it as such: an audio tokenizer, held by the processor next to the text tokenizer:

A voice is not a recording but a tensor of speaker latents. Phonon never encodes audio directly with its audio tokenizer, which ships decoder-only, and voices come precomputed: gradium/phonon-voices.

The prompt layout (voice positions, text, then a token opening the audio) ships with the checkpoint as a chat template, as for other multimodal models in Transformers. You write a standard conversation, with an empty audio item where the voice goes, and your code stays the same across checkpoints. The processor then expands the voice placeholder to one position per frame, normalizes and tokenizes the text, and batches the inputs:

generate returns latents, which the processor decodes to audio:

Phonon can speak with any voice. Clone one from a short recording with the speaker’s consent, or describe a new one in plain text in Gradium Studio. Then download the voice file, load it in Phonon, and it runs fully on the device.

We also train custom Phonon models with design partners. If your memory budget is tight, we can make the model smaller. If you need Korean, Arabic or Japanese, we can train for that too. And if your product has its own vocabulary, we can fine-tune on it. Get in touch and tell us what you need.

Thank you to the Hugging Face team, and to everyone who tried Phonon in its first two weeks.

Phonon is our first open release. Try it out and tell us what you build.

#9712. My Worker Exited 0 With Jobs Still Marked "Running", and Nothing Retried Them

A deploy finished at 02:10, the supervisor logged a clean stop, and the worker exited with code 0. By 02:12 the queue depth graph was flat at zero, which looked like success and was actually the opposite. Work had been claimed, never finished, and the rows sat in running where no retry could see them. So what exactly happens to a job that is mid-flight when the platform sends SIGTERM?

My worker loop claims one row at a time from a jobs table, calls one outbound HTTP endpoint, then marks the row done. Each call has a 20-second client timeout, and the orchestrator allows 10 seconds between SIGTERM and SIGKILL. That mismatch alone guarantees the drain can never finish, but three smaller decisions turned it into a silent data problem instead of a loud crash.

Put those together and the failing path is boring: signal arrives, handler flips a flag, the main thread is still blocked inside a 20-second socket read, SIGKILL lands, and the row keeps status='running' for half an hour. Is your shutdown path covered by any test at all, or only by the deploy that happens to be quiet?

The useful part of this bug is that it is cheap to reproduce, because you only need real signals and a real process table. Save the worker as worker.py, then drive it from this script:

And inspect.py is deliberately dumb, because you want it to fail loudly:

Run it against the naive worker and you should see exactly the number of jobs that were in flight when the kill landed. Run it against a fixed worker and the count should be zero, or the rows should already be back in queued before your script checks. Label: the SQL below is reconstructed pseudo-Postgres, not a copy of production code; adapt the claim statement to your own store.

The first temptation is to "handle the signal properly", which does not help when the kill arrives mid-socket. The version that survived my next deploy had three parts.

The reaper then becomes a one-liner you can reason about, and its window is bounded by the heartbeat interval rather than by a 30-minute guess:

Keep the lease comfortably larger than the heartbeat plus the slowest single call, and check the numbers instead of vibes. One caveat that bit me: do not reuse the main connection inside the heartbeat thread, because most drivers are not thread-safe and you will get a confusing protocol error that looks like a database bug.

The shutdown deadline, the per-job timeout, and the platform grace period are three numbers that must agree, and I now write them in one table before touching the code.

If the platform grace is shorter than your worst-case drain, stop pretending you can drain: shorten the per-job timeout, cut concurrency to one at a time, and let the lease do the recovery work. Which of those three numbers did you actually measure, and which one did you copy from a sample config file?

Two parts of this loop are annoying to set up on a laptop, so I used MonkeyCode's free model access and free server option for them. Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach. The free model was decent at the tedious part, turning a few thousand lines of claim/release log lines into an ordered timeline of stop_requested, last heartbeat, and kill, which is exactly the reading I am worst at doing patiently. The free server gave me a plain Linux shell where kill -TERM hits a real process and wait returns a real exit code, which is the whole point of the harness above.

What it did not do is decide the deadline numbers or tell me the reaper window was wrong, because a model reading logs only sees what I logged. The honest limitation is that if your worker never emits in_flight, no amount of summarising will recover it, so fix the log line first and paste it second.

The changes I would keep tomorrow are the harness (it runs in CI as a smoke test), the lease column with a heartbeat, and the event=stopped_with_work line that a grep can find during a post-deploy check. The sprint I would not repeat is the hour I spent adding a longer SIGTERM handler, which cannot help a thread that is blocked in a socket read.

Skip this approach if you are on a runtime with no signal semantics, if your grace period is under a second, or if you cannot add a lease column and a reaper. Also skip it if you need exactly-once processing, because a lease gives you at-least-once and your handler still has to be idempotent. If you want to rerun the harness without provisioning your own box, the free server option is a reasonable place to start, and the code above is the part worth copying.

#9711. The Clothes That Make People Appear More Intelligent

How to use clothes to appear more competent.

How to use clothes to appear more competent.

Wearing more clothing makes you look more competent, a study finds.

Something as simple as taking off a sweater is enough to make you look less competent, the researchers found.

The finding applies to both men and women, said Dr Kurt Gray, the study’s first author:

“An important thing about our study is that, unlike much previous research, ours applies to both sexes.

It also calls into question the nature of objectification because people without clothes are not seen as mindless objects, but they are instead attributed a different kind of mind.”

The effect occurs because seeing more flesh encourages us to think about a person’s body, rather than their mind.

“We also show that this effect can happen even without the removal of clothes.

Simply focusing on someone’s attractiveness, in essence concentrating on their body rather than their mind, makes you see her or him as less of an agent [someone who acts and plans] more of an experiencer.”

Showing bare skin, though, does have some advantages, explained Dr Gray:

“A focus on the body, and the increased perception of sensitivity and emotion it elicits might be good for lovers in the bedroom.

Others appear to be less inclined to harm people with bare skin and more inclined to protect them.

In one experiment, for example, people viewing male subjects with their shirts off were less inclined to give those subjects uncomfortable electric shocks than when the men had their shirts on.”

“Even more than robbing someone of agency, the increased experience that may accompany body perceptions may lead those who are characterized in terms of their bodies to be seen as more reactive and emotional, traits that may also serve to work against career advancement.”

The study was published in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology (Gray et al., 2011).

#9710. Debugging macOS LaunchAgent Failures With launchctl and Exit Code 78

Head of Revenue Operations. Revenue analytics, sales ops, and the SQL behind both. Atlanta.

Head of Revenue Operations. Revenue analytics, sales ops, and the SQL behind both. Atlanta.

Head of Revenue Operations. Revenue analytics, sales ops, and the SQL behind both. Atlanta.

Every morning at 7:45, a job on my Mac runs a reconciliation and posts the results for the finance team. It's an ordinary LaunchAgent: a plist in ~/Library/LaunchAgents, a Python script, and a log file.

For three mornings in October, it didn't run.

Nothing told me. There was no error in Slack, because the code that sends errors never started. There was no crash report. And the log file, the first place anyone looks, had nothing new in it, because the job failed before it could write a line.

launchd keeps a record of every job's last exit. Ask for it:

The labels in this post are examples. For a quick look at every job, launchctl list shows the last exit status in its second column.

78 is EX_CONFIG from sysexits.h, a configuration error. My script never exits with 78, and that's the tell: when the exit code is one your program doesn't use, your program probably never ran.

Before launchd starts your program, it does some setup. It opens the files named in StandardOutPath and StandardErrorPath, changes into WorkingDirectory, and finds the executable. If any of that fails, your program never starts, and the job ends with 78.

I wanted to know exactly which mistakes produce it, so I loaded a set of deliberately broken test jobs on macOS 26.6 and read what launchd reported:

Two things surprised me. launchd happily creates a missing log folder, so that's not your problem. And a log file it can't open is fatal. Not a warning and not a quiet fallback: the whole job stops, and the error has nowhere to go.

The worst part of debugging a 7:45 job is the 23-hour feedback loop. You don't need it. Copy the plist, give it a new label, swap the program for something harmless, and tell it to run at load. Everything launchd sets up stays the same, so if the setup is broken, you'll see 78 in two seconds:

/usr/bin/true does nothing and exits 0. If the copy still reports 78, the problem is in the setup, not your code. Fix the plist, rerun the copy, and only then touch the real job. Reload the real one with launchctl bootout and launchctl bootstrap so launchd reads the new version.

Once I'd found one of these, I wanted to check the rest. This script reads every plist in ~/Library/LaunchAgents, flags the setups that end in 78, and prints each job's last exit code:

crm-sync is the classic upgrade casualty: Python moved, and the plist still points at the old interpreter. weekly-export is a renamed folder. Both fail silently in exactly the same way mine did, and cash-recon gets flagged before it ever has the chance.

The fix took five minutes. Noticing took three days, because every alert I had lived inside the job, and the job never ran. A job that doesn't start can't report its own failure.

What would have caught it on the first morning is a check that doesn't depend on the job at all: something separate that looks for the job's last success and complains when it's missing. It's the same principle I wrote about in small pipelines fail quietly: watch for the last success, not the last error.

The short version, for every LaunchAgent you rely on:

Your GitHub Actions Cron Job Can Disappear Without Failing

#9709. New NVIDIA Cosmos 3 Open Models for Interactive World Simulation

NVIDIA Cosmos world model development platform adds four new open-weight checkpoints to its Cosmos 3 model family for generating interactive world simulation and multi-sensor multi-view driving scenes:

All four models are post-trained examples of Cosmos 3 Nano and have 16B trainable parameters. The models use OpenMDW1.1, permitting commercial and non-commercial use under its terms.

Download the checkpoints · Read the technical report . Watch the demos

🦾 Robotics needs environments that can answer this across changing scenes and viewpoints. These checkpoints offer complementary ways to build them: Sim-Bimanual predicts visual consequences from actions, while Sim-Transfer turns a physics simulator’s controls into generated observations.

🚦 For autonomous driving, appearance and geometry must agree. Synchronized camera and LiDAR generation connects visual observations with 3D sensing. Scene and traffic-signal controls let researchers vary road layouts and signal states, then study how a driving policy responds.

🔄 Each observation can shape the next action. Streaming generation connects video prediction to ongoing interaction, giving world-model researchers a way to explore how actions and observations unfold together.

🌐 An open foundation for others to build on. NVIDIA’s vision is to help researchers and developers create richer, more responsive simulated worlds. Open weights and post-training recipes provide a shared starting point for adapting models, comparing methods, and contributing improvements. These problems remain hard: the work ahead is to measure where the models faithfully support policy learning and evaluation, understand their limits, and improve where they fall short.

Cosmos3-Nano-Transfer-Auto is a bidirectional model for offline synthetic driving data generation. It generates synchronized video across up to 11 camera views, including fisheyes, and supports joint RGB–LiDAR generation. Per-camera World Scenario Map (WSM) controls specify scene structure and traffic motion, while text prompts guide appearance.

Developers can vary environmental conditions to expand training and evaluation coverage, with optional initial RGB images to anchor scene appearance. Joint LiDAR generation additionally uses aligned HD-map range-map controls. Transfer-Auto also serves as the foundation for adapting Cosmos to your own sensor rig and driving domain. Start by post-training it on your data to accommodate your camera layout, LiDAR configuration, and target environment. The adapted model can be used directly for offline data generation or undergo causal training and few-step distillation for fast streaming simulation—the development path used to create Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Auto.

Point your agent to the open skill : Run inference with Cosmos3-Nano-Transfer-Auto

Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Auto is the causally distilled streaming variant of Transfer-Auto. It generates successive small chunks of synchronized camera video and LiDAR in just a few denoising steps, using generated history and updated driving controls to support fast streaming and long, interactive rollouts.

Provide per-camera captions and synchronized WSM controls, optionally adding initial RGB images. For LiDAR generation, include HD-Map range controls aligned with the camera controls. The distilled model generates successive chunks using its rolling history. Closed-loop interaction requires a simulation runtime and WSM renderer to update those controls from driving inputs. For a new sensor rig or domain, adapt Transfer-Auto first, then distill it into Sim-Auto.

Point your agent to the open skill : Run inference with Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Auto

Your simulator computes motion, contacts, and physical state. Sim-Transfer uses its spatial controls and a text prompt to render color observations that a policy can consume.

Action → simulator update → spatial controls → generated RGB → next policy action

Depth: relative distance from the camera.

Segmentation: regions and object boundaries.

Text guides appearance; physics and ground-truth state stay with the simulator.

Point your agent to the open skill : Run inference with Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Transfer

Output Video From Sim-Bimanual Simulation Checkpoint

Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Bimanual simulates how an environment evolves in response to a bimanual robot’s actions. It supports interactive two-arm simulation for YAM and AgiBot embodiments, controlled by a policy or human-operated joysticks.

Start with an image, move the robot or camera, and generate the next observations. One control sequence can switch between viewpoint changes and manipulation.

The mixed-action example uses 59 control values, padded to 64 during training. Its schema defines coordinate frames, rotations, gripper calibration, validity masks, and control domains. Follow those conventions so each value describes the intended motion.

Keep timing aligned: T transitions need T+1 observations. Training transforms raw captures into the model’s action representation; released inference actions are already normalized.

Here, Sim-Transfer generates visuals from a physics simulator’s updated state; Sim-Bimanual generates the next observation directly from the scene and robot actions.

Requirements: Linux, an NVIDIA GPU, Docker, and NVIDIA Container Toolkit. The published vLLM-Omni setup was tested on one GB200; this is not a minimum-memory specification. The server downloads weights; the clients fetch sample inputs.

Point your agent to the open skill : Run inference with Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Bimanual

Cosmos 3’s Mixture-of-Transformers backbone connects separate text-processing and visual-generation networks through attention. The generator predicts each short segment from the prompt, available controls, and generated history.

Controls + history → generate chunk → decode images → update history

Denoising refines noisy, compressed video representations into a segment. Temporal-causal attention lets it read available history and controls while blocking future target observations. A key/value cache retains attention information for the next prediction.

The model operates on compressed video representations called latents. After the initial image, each latent time step represents four RGB frames. Transfer predicts one step per chunk; the optimized Bimanual setup in the report predicts two. Smaller chunks let new controls affect generation more often.

Stage 0 — Bidirectional adaptation: learn the domain and its control-to-video relationships from complete recorded clips.

Stage 1 — Teacher forcing: predict each chunk from earlier recorded observations and available controls, with the clean answer and future targets masked out.

Stage 2 — Consistency distillation: use a frozen teacher to train a student that generates each chunk in four denoising steps.

Stage 3 — Self-forcing: train on the student’s generated history. A frozen teacher and an auxiliary score model supply the distribution-matching signal.

Why the final stage matters: a slightly mispredicted object becomes context for later frames, so errors can compound. Self-forcing exposes training to that generated history. Distillation and caching reduce the cost of producing each observation.

The post-training recipes start from Cosmos3-Nano or compatible base weights and cover all four stages. Keep full training checkpoints to resume; exported inference weights omit optimizer and other training state.

Transfer-auto: Post-train on your driving data to adapt to your sensor rig and domain, and generate offline synthetic data.

Sim-auto: Apply causal training and distillation to an adapted Transfer-Auto model for fast streaming simulation.

Sim-Transfer : Post-train the checkpoint for your environment with local data preparation, stage configurations, and resume.

Sim-Bimanual: Post-train for your embodiment with data validation, stage configurations, checkpoint handoffs, and export.

Give your coding agent the skill and dataset location. Follow the environment checks, validate a sample, and test training and restart before a longer run. Evaluate quality on held-out episodes: a successful short run verifies execution, not convergence.

#9708. Your Free Tier Is Not a Capacity Plan: Five Throughput Myths and a Concurrency Ramp

A demo handles one request at a time. A launch sends ten at once. The endpoint falls over.

Was the model worse today? Or did nobody measure the shape of the curve?

I keep seeing the same five claims about free models and free servers. Each one sounds reasonable. Each one falls apart under a ten-minute test.

I run these probes against MonkeyCode's free model access and its free server option while prototyping.

Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach.

Nothing below depends on that relationship. Swap in any endpoint you control. The method is the point.

If one call takes two seconds, ten calls take twenty. Right?

No. That is a queue, not a multiplier. Little's Law says concurrency equals arrival rate multiplied by time in system. When arrivals outrun service capacity, waiting time stops being bounded.

The curve has a knee. Left of it, latency is flat. Right of it, latency goes vertical and errors appear.

You cannot read the knee in a doc page. You find it by ramping.

Retries feel like resilience. Under saturation they are a load multiplier.

Say a third of calls fail and you retry twice. Offered load can nearly double. At the knee, that turns a brownout into an outage.

A corrected model: retry only classified transient failures. Use exponential backoff with jitter. Keep a retry budget, something like ten percent of successful calls.

Primary sources worth reading: AWS on backoff and jitter and the SRE book chapter on handling overload.

Free tiers make people skip measurement. "It is just a prototype."

But the shape transfers. The knee moves. The existence of a knee does not.

A prototype that dies at ten users teaches you nothing. A prototype with a written envelope teaches you where the queue belongs.

A 429 is admission control talking. It says your offered load exceeded what the server will accept.

A timeout says your deadline was shorter than time to first byte.

Neither one is a bug report. Both are signals to slow down, queue, or shed.

Make 429 a first-class state in the client. Do not swallow it as an exception.

Without all five numbers, "the model is slow" is a guess with good manners.

Here is the probe. It is a template, not a run. I am not publishing numbers from it.

Stop rule first. Stop a level when either condition fires:

If rps flattens while p95 climbs, you are past the knee. More concurrency is now just more waiting.

Half the knee, not the knee. Headroom is for the day your prompt gets longer.

Now encode what you measured. Do not leave it in a notebook.

Retryable is yours to define. Map 429, 503, and connect timeouts to it. Map everything else to a hard failure.

So why ship a cap you never measured? You cannot defend a number you never took.

Run one ramp. Write the knee in your README. If you are prototyping on a budget, run the same script against MonkeyCode's free model access and free server option before you commit to a paid plan. The script does not care whose endpoint answers.

#9707. Building Data Observability for Banking Pipelines

Data Engineer specialising in Azure, AWS, Databricks, dbt, and scalable data platforms. Writing about Data Engineering, AI, and cloud architecture.

Data Engineer specialising in Azure, AWS, Databricks, dbt, and scalable data platforms. Writing about Data Engineering, AI, and cloud architecture.

Data Engineer specialising in Azure, AWS, Databricks, dbt, and scalable data platforms. Writing about Data Engineering, AI, and cloud architecture.

Loud failures are easy. A job crashes, the scheduler turns red, somebody gets paged, and within the hour there is a chat thread with far too many people in it. Annoying, sure, but the system is at least telling you the truth.

The failure I worry about is the quiet one. Every task shows green. The report lands on time. And one number inside it is wrong, because a feed stopped refreshing three days ago or a join started dropping rows, and nothing in the stack was built to care.

In most industries that is an embarrassing dashboard. In banking it can turn into a regulatory submission, a liquidity figure in front of a risk committee, or a customer statement. The stakes shift quite a lot. So this piece is about silent failures: what they look like, why banks are unusually exposed to them, and a way of building observability that catches them before a report breaks. I should say early that it will not catch everything. I'll come back to what it misses.

I can think of three reasons, though there are probably more.

First, the chains are long. A single regulatory figure, say a liquidity coverage ratio, might pass through a core banking extract, a treasury system, a reference data service, a staging layer, a transformation layer and finally a reporting tool. Each hop belongs to someone else, often with a release calendar nobody downstream has seen.

Second, banks lean heavily on batch. Plenty of critical feeds arrive once a day, and some only once a month. If a daily feed breaks on Tuesday, you might not see the damage until the Friday reconciliation, or the month-end close. A long feedback loop gives bad data plenty of time to travel.

Third, and this is the uncomfortable one, a lot of existing monitoring answers the question "did the job run?" when the question that matters is "is the data right?" Those are different questions. A job can run perfectly and load nothing at all.

None of the following is a real incident from a named bank, but the shapes are familiar to anyone who has worked near a data warehouse.

The stale rate table. An FX rates feed from a market data vendor stops updating after a change on the vendor side. Your pipeline keeps reading the table, which still has plenty of rows, so the job-level check passes. Euro and dollar positions get converted at last Wednesday's rate. Totals look sensible. They just are not true.

The shrinking join. An upstream team changes a code in a product reference table, perhaps a new product type with no mapping yet. An inner join quietly drops everything that no longer matches. Three percent of the loan book disappears from a report. Three percent does not look dramatic on a chart. In a capital calculation, it might be very dramatic.

The drifting distribution. A source system starts defaulting a null field, like days past due, to zero. Row counts are identical. The schema is identical. But the share of loans classed as current jumps overnight, and nobody changed a credit policy.

None of these throws an exception. All of them pass a "job succeeded" check.

I'm a bit wary of the word "observability" because vendors have stretched it until it covers almost anything. The distinction I find useful is simple. Monitoring checks things you already know can go wrong. Observability means collecting enough information about the data itself, continuously, that when something strange happens you can work out where it started and what it touched.

For data, that mostly means watching the data and not only the machinery. CPU on the warehouse tells you very little about whether the FX table is current.

There are lots of ways to slice this. The five below are the ones I keep coming back to, partly because each maps neatly to one of the failures above.

Freshness. When did this table last change, compared with when it should have? One trap here: check the business date inside the data, not the load timestamp. A job can load yesterday's rates today and look perfectly fresh by the wrong clock. That is exactly how the stale rate table slips through.

Volume. Are row counts in a plausible range? The word that matters is plausible, because banks have calendars. UK bank holidays, month-end, quarter-end and year-end all change expected volumes. A check that ignores them will cry wolf every few weeks, and people will stop listening.

Schema. Have columns been added, dropped or retyped? This is the cheapest signal to collect and often the most useful, since a renamed column is a common cause of everything downstream going subtly wrong.

Distribution. Null rates, value ranges, category proportions, and sums of balances. This is where the drifting distribution gets caught. It is also the noisiest signal, so I would introduce it last.

Lineage. Which reports depend on this table? When a check fails, lineage tells you the blast radius. Without it, the alert reads "something is odd in staging" and everyone shrugs. With it, the alert reads "something is odd in staging, and it feeds the liquidity report due at 10am". That is a very different conversation.

Here is the layout I would sketch on a whiteboard. The main idea is that checks live at the boundaries between layers, not only at the end next to the report.

Reading it left to right, the data moves from source systems through ingestion, raw storage, staging, curated marts, and finally the regulatory and management reports. Underneath, an observability layer attaches a different kind of check to each stage.

At ingestion, you ask the cheap questions: did the file arrive, is it fresh by business date, does the schema match the agreed contract? In staging, you look at keys, referential integrity and null rates. In the marts, you run reconciliations and distribution checks. At the report layer, you compare control totals against the prior period and against the general ledger.

Reconciliation deserves a special mention because it is old-fashioned and brilliant. Finance teams have done it for decades. The idea is that the sum of balances in your mart should equal the sum in the source extract, within a tolerance. If a join drops three percent of the loan book, a control total notices immediately, even though row counts and schemas look fine. Plenty of data teams skip it because it feels unglamorous. I would start there.

Every check writes its result to a metadata store. That store feeds the alerting layer and, ideally, a lineage graph, so a failure can be traced to the reports it threatens.

A small example of the volume check, written as plain SQL so it is easy to port. It compares the latest day against the same weekday over the past eight weeks. Treat it as a sketch rather than production code, because it knows nothing about holidays yet.

If the z-score goes past something like 3, raise a flag. The threshold is a guess you will tune, and you should expect to be wrong about it the first few times.

Collecting signals is the easy half. The harder half is making sure a human reacts to them.

I have seen, or at least heard enough war stories to believe in, the pattern where a team switches on two hundred checks, gets forty alerts a day, and within a month has muted the channel. At that point you have built an expensive way of generating noise. So the design question is less "what can we check?" and more "what deserves to interrupt someone?"

A scheme that tends to hold up has three tiers. Informational checks get logged and reviewed weekly. Warnings go to the named owner of the dataset during working hours. Critical failures, meaning anything that touches a regulatory report, go to the owner immediately and also close a gate in front of the publish step.

That gate is the controversial part. Some teams prefer to publish anyway with a visible warning banner, on the argument that a late report is worse than a flagged one. Others hold the previous approved version until someone signs off. I lean towards holding for regulatory outputs and warning for internal dashboards, but I can see the other side. If your submission deadline is fixed by a regulator, the calculation changes.

Whichever way you go, two things matter more than the tooling. Every dataset needs a named owner, a person and not a shared inbox. And upstream teams need a lightweight data contract, even a one-page agreement, saying which columns and codes they promise not to change without notice. Without that, you are monitoring someone else's decisions with no way to influence them.

I would be overselling it if I stopped there.

Observability catches data that is stale, missing, malformed or oddly distributed. It does not catch data that is fresh, complete, consistent and simply wrong because the business logic misreads a rule. A risk weight applied to the wrong asset class will sail through every check described above. That needs code review, testing and domain experts, and no dashboard replaces them.

Thresholds can also create false confidence. A check tuned so loosely that it never fires is worse than no check, because people assume it is protecting them. Anomaly detection tools driven by machine learning can help with tuning, but I am slightly cautious about them in a regulated setting. An auditor can read a rule that says "volume within three standard deviations of the weekday baseline". A black box that quietly adapts its own thresholds is harder to defend.

And then there is the organisational side, which no architecture diagram captures. If upstream teams see your alerts as an accusation and not a courtesy, the checks will be ignored. A bit of diplomacy goes a long way here.

If I were starting on Monday, I would not try to cover the whole warehouse. I would pick one regulatory report, trace its lineage back to the ten or so tables it truly depends on, and add three things: freshness by business date, a volume check with a calendar, and a control total that reconciles to source.

Then I would assign owners and run everything in warn-only mode for two weeks. That gives you a feel for false positives before anyone is woken up at night. Only after that would I switch the critical checks to blocking.

That staged approach is slower than a big-bang rollout, and some teams will find it frustrating. But it builds trust in the alerts, and trust is the thing that decides whether anyone responds when the real one fires.

Silent failures are hard because they look like success. The pipeline is green, the report is on time, and the number is wrong. Catching them means shifting attention from whether the job ran to whether the data still makes sense, and doing it at every boundary, not just at the finish line.

None of this is exotic. Freshness, volume, schema, distribution, lineage, plus a few reconciliations that finance has trusted for decades. The hard parts are the unglamorous ones: ownership, contracts, tuning thresholds and keeping the noise low enough that people still care. If your team is working through the same problem, I would be curious which of the five signals you found most useful in practice. My bet is freshness by business date, but I could easily be wrong.

#9706. Building a Charge Page Template for a Criminal Defense Site

If you build or maintain a website for a criminal defense firm, most of your work will end up in one template: the charge page. A typical defense site has twenty to sixty of them, one for each offense the firm handles, sometimes split by county or by first and repeat offenses. They bring in most of the search traffic and most of the calls.

A good charge page template makes those pages easy for lawyers and editors to write, consistent for readers and fast on a phone. A weak one turns every new page into a custom design job. This post covers how to design the template from the content model up, with notes from the kinds of problems that show up on real law firm sites.

Before opening a design tool, define the fields a charge page needs. Lawyers think in terms of the charge, the possible penalties, the court process and common defenses. The CMS should reflect that so editors fill in structured fields rather than one large rich text box.

The last_reviewed field matters more than it looks. Penalties and procedures change, and a visible review date helps both readers and the firm keep pages accurate.

Most people reach a charge page from a phone, often in a stressful moment. The first screen should show the charge name as the heading, a short opening that speaks to the reader's situation and a clear way to call. Large hero images push all of that below the fold, so keep them small or leave them out.

Each field in the content model should map to a section component with fixed styling. Editors choose the content, not the fonts, colors or spacing. That keeps forty charge pages looking like one site rather than forty experiments.

Navigation matters as the number of charge pages grows. This guide on building a menu for a defense firm with many practice areas covers how to group charges so visitors and crawlers can find them.

Charge pages compete in local search, and page experience is part of what Google considers. Watch the Core Web Vitals: Largest Contentful Paint, Interaction to Next Paint and Cumulative Layout Shift. On law firm sites, the usual causes of trouble are oversized hero images, chat widgets that load early and block the main thread, and fonts or embeds that shift the layout as they load.

Set explicit dimensions on images and embeds. Load third-party chat and tracking scripts after the main content. Self-host fonts or limit the number of weights. Test on a mid-range Android phone over a throttled connection rather than only on a fast laptop.

Lawyers need to review penalty and process content before it goes live. Build a draft and review state into the CMS workflow, and record who approved each page. Attorney advertising rules vary by state, and some require disclaimers on certain pages. Add a disclaimer field or a site-wide component that can be switched on per page rather than hard-coding text.

Accessibility belongs in the template too. Use proper heading order, sufficient color contrast and form labels that screen readers can announce. A person in crisis may be using assistive technology, and an inaccessible contact form loses calls.

For more design ideas aimed at defense practices, see the collection of law firm website design guides.

No. A shared template with structured fields keeps the site consistent and makes maintenance far easier. Variation should come from the content.

Use the same template with a jurisdiction field and require unique local content, such as the courthouse and local process, so the pages are not near-duplicates.

Generate it from the structured fields so it stays in sync with the visible content. Only mark up what is actually on the page.

SBD Marketing works only with criminal defense law firms, one firm per city. It helps them with website design, SEO for the charges they defend, visibility in AI search tools and SEO audits.

#9705. A Nasty Sign Of Omega-3 Deficiency

A high omega-3 diet can lower the signs and symptoms of the disease by 50 per cent.

A high omega-3 diet can lower the signs and symptoms of the disease by 50 per cent.

Stiffness in the joints and swelling can be indirect signs of omega-3 deficiency, research suggests.

Waking up stiff in the morning, feeling pain in the joints, swelling, tenderness and loss of flexibility are all signs of arthritis.

Omega-3 deficiency could be contributing, as scientists believe there is a link between this leading cause of disability and a lack of omega-3 in the diet.

Researchers suggest that a diet rich in omega-3 could decrease the symptoms of osteoarthritis.

A study has found that adding fish oil to the diet — and to some degree flaxseed oil (alpha-linolenic acid has an anti-inflammatory effect) — can ease or even prevent osteoarthritis.

With population aging, osteoarthritis will be one of the leading causes of disability.

According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, by 2040 it is estimated that 26% of US adults aged 18 or older will be diagnosed by a doctor with arthritis.

While there are still no effective medications for treating this condition, omega-3 fish oil can be one of the best natural remedies in treating osteoarthritis.

Professor John Tarlton, the lead researcher of the study, explained the effect of omega-3 on osteoarthritis:

“Classic early signs of the condition, such as the degradation of collagen in cartilage and the loss of molecules that give it shock-absorbing properties, were both reduced with omega-3.

Furthermore, there was strong evidence that omega-3 influences the biochemistry of the disease, and therefore not only helps prevent disease, but also slows its progression, potentially controlling established osteoarthritis.”

Western diets contain high levels of omega-6 fatty acids, which can lead to inflammatory disorders such as colitis, heart disease, osteoporosis, cancer, rheumatoid arthritis and osteoarthritis.

Modern diets contain up to 30 times more omega-6 than omega-3, whereas our ancestor’s diets contained almost an equal level of these two omega fatty acids.

Therefore, supplementation with omega-3 can help to restore this imbalance in Western diets and improve conditions such as colitis and heart-related diseases.

Fish oil is much more effective than flax seed oil, but for vegetarians and vegans this supplement is an important option.

“Most diets in the developed world are lacking in omega-3, with modern diets having up to 30 times too much omega-6 and too little omega-3.

Taking omega-3 will help redress this imbalance and may positively contribute to a range of other health problems such as heart disease and colitis.”

The study was published in the journal of Osteoarthritis and Cartilage (Knott et al., 2011).

In this guide, I'm going to help you learn more about these SEO tools and how to choose the one that's best for your purposes.

SEMrush is a popular SEO tool with a wide range of features—it's the leading competitor research service for online marketers. SEMrush's SEO Keyword Magic tool offers over 20 billion Google-approved keywords, which are constantly updated and it's the largest keyword database.

The program was developed in 2007 as SeoQuake is a small Firefox extension

Ahrefs is a leading SEO platform that offers a set of tools to grow your search traffic, research your competitors, and monitor your niche. The company was founded in 2010, and it has become a popular choice among SEO tools. Ahrefs has a keyword index of over 10.3 billion keywords and offers accurate and extensive backlink data updated every 15-30 minutes and it is the world's most extensive backlink index database.

Now that you know a little more about each tool, let's take a look at how they compare. I'll analyze each tool to see how they differ in interfaces, keyword research resources, rank tracking, and competitor analysis.

Ahrefs and SEMrush both offer comprehensive information and quick metrics regarding your website's SEO performance. However, Ahrefs takes a bit more of a hands-on approach to getting your account fully set up, whereas SEMrush's simpler dashboard can give you access to the data you need quickly.

In this section, we provide a brief overview of the elements found on each dashboard and highlight the ease with which you can complete tasks.

The Ahrefs dashboard is less cluttered than that of SEMrush, and its primary menu is at the very top of the page, with a search bar designed only for entering URLs.

Additional features of the Ahrefs platform include:

When you log into the SEMrush Tool, you will find four main modules. These include information about your domains, organic keyword analysis, ad keyword, and site traffic.

Both Ahrefs and SEMrush have user-friendly dashboards, but Ahrefs is less cluttered and easier to navigate. On the other hand, SEMrush offers dozens of extra tools, including access to customer support resources.

When deciding on which dashboard to use, consider what you value in the user interface, and test out both.

If you're looking to track your website's search engine ranking, rank tracking features can help. You can also use them to monitor your competitors.

Let's take a look at Ahrefs vs. SEMrush to see which tool does a better job.

The Ahrefs Rank Tracker is simpler to use. Just type in the domain name and keywords you want to analyze, and it spits out a report showing you the search engine results page (SERP) ranking for each keyword you enter.

Rank Tracker looks at the ranking performance of keywords and compares them with the top rankings for those keywords. Ahrefs also offers:

You'll see metrics that help you understand your visibility, traffic, average position, and keyword difficulty.

It gives you an idea of whether a keyword would be profitable to target or not.

SEMRush offers a tool called Position Tracking. This tool is a project tool—you must set it up as a new project. Below are a few of the most popular features of the SEMrush Position Tracking tool:

The platform provides opportunities to track several SERP features, including Local tracking.

Intuitive reports allow you to track statistics for the pages on your website, as well as the keywords used in those pages.

Identify pages that may be competing with each other using the Cannibalization report.

Ahrefs is a more user-friendly option. It takes seconds to enter a domain name and keywords. From there, you can quickly decide whether to proceed with that keyword or figure out how to rank better for other keywords.

Keyword research is closely related to rank tracking, but it's used for deciding which keywords you plan on using for future content rather than those you use now.

When it comes to SEO, keyword research is the most important thing to consider when comparing the two platforms.

The Ahrefs Keyword Explorer provides you with thousands of keyword ideas and filters search results based on the chosen search engine.

Ahrefs supports several features, including:

SEMrush's Keyword Magic Tool has over 20 billion keywords for Google. You can type in any keyword you want, and a list of suggested keywords will appear.

If you're interested in keyword suggestions, SEMrush appears to have more keyword suggestions than Ahrefs does. It also continues to add new features, like the Keyword Gap tool and SERP Questions recommendations.

What is Sellfy?

Sellfy is an eCommerce solution that allows digital content creators, including writers, illustrators, designers, musicians, and filmmakers, to sell their products online. Sellfy provides a customizable storefront where users can display their digital products and embed "Buy Now" buttons on their website or blog. Sellfy product pages enable users to showcase their products from different angles with multiple images and previews from Soundcloud, Vimeo, and YouTube. Users can also embed their entire store or individual project widgets in their site, with the ability to preview how widgets will appear before they are displayed.

Features

Sellfy includes:

Online Store

Sellfy also allows you to create a full shopping cart so customers can purchase multiple items. And Sellfy gives you the ability to set your language or let customers see a translated version of your store based on their location.

Sellfy gives you the option to host your store directly on its platform, add a custom domain to your store, and use it as an embedded storefront on your website. Sellfy also optimizes its store offerings for mobile devices, allowing for a seamless checkout experience.

Product hosting

Sellfy also does not place storage limits on your store but recommends that files be no larger than 5GB. This option allows you to give customers control over the cost of individual items (without a minimum price) or to set pricing minimums—a good option if you're in a competitive market or when you have higher-end products. Sellfy is ideal for selling digital content, such as ebooks. But it does not allow you to copyrighted material (that you don't have rights to distribute).

Embed options

Sellfy lets you integrate it with your existing website using "buy now" buttons, embed your entire storefront, or embed certain products so you can reach more people. Sellfy also enables you to connect with your Facebook page and YouTube channel, maximizing your visibility.

Payments and security

Sellfy is a simple online platform that allows customers to buy your products directly through your store. Sellfy has two payment processing options: PayPal and Stripe. You will receive instant payments with both of these processors, and your customer data is protected by Sellfy's secure (PCI-compliant) payment security measures. In addition to payment security, Sellfy provides anti-fraud tools to help protect your products including PDF stamping, unique download links, and limited download attempts.


Marketing and analytics tools

The Sellfy platform includes marketing and analytics tools to help you manage your online store. You can send email product updates and collect newsletter subscribers through the platform. With Sellfy, you can also offer discount codes and product upsells, as well as create and track Facebook and Twitter ads for your store. The software's analytics dashboard will help you track your best-performing products, generated revenue, traffic channels, top locations, and overall store performance.

Integrations

Google Analytics and Webhooks, as well as integrations with Patreon and Facebook Live Chat, are just a few of the options available.
